title: Lockout/tagout: the six steps
hazard: A machine that starts up or releases energy while someone is working on it can crush, cut, burn or shock that person.
key_points: Know every energy source the machine has, and tell the people who run or work near it before you shut it down.
Shut the machine down the normal way, then operate every disconnect, valve or breaker that feeds it.
Lock out only if you are trained and authorized, and put your own lock and tag on each energy isolating device.
Release or block stored energy like springs, air, hydraulics and raised parts.
Make sure everyone is clear, then try the normal start controls to prove it will not run, and return them to off.
Follow your site's written lockout procedure for that specific machine.
must_say: Never remove someone else's lock.
If it is not locked out, keep your hands and body out.
never_say: Hitting the stop button is the same as locking out.
A quick job doesn't need a lock if you are fast.
It's fine to borrow a coworker's lock or put your lock on for someone else.

facts.text: Lockout steps must be done in order: prepare, shut down, isolate, apply locks or tags, control stored energy, then verify isolation.
Each lock or tag must be removed by the employee who put it on, except under special employer procedures when that person is not available.
Before work starts, the authorized employee must verify that the machine is isolated and de-energized.

story_seed: A mechanic shut off a mixer at the panel but skipped the lock because the job was 'two minutes.' A coworker on the next shift saw the panel off, assumed it was a mistake, and reached for the switch before someone shouted.
crew_questions: Which machine in our area has more than one energy source, and do we know where every disconnect is?
When was the last time a job here felt too quick to lock out, and what should we have done?

title: Group lockout and shift changes
hazard: When a crew works on one machine or a job runs across shifts, a person can be left unprotected if locks come off or change hands the wrong way.
key_points: Put your own personal lock on the group lockbox or group device when you start work.
Take off only your own lock, and only when you stop working on that machine.
Know who the authorized person in charge of the group lockout is.
At shift change, follow your site's procedure so oncoming locks go on before off-going locks come off.
Never assume the machine is safe because other locks are already on it.
must_say: Your own lock protects you. Put it on the group lockbox every time.
Never remove someone else's lock.
never_say: One lock for the whole crew is enough.
The off-going shift can pull their locks first and the next shift locks on after.
A supervisor's lock covers everyone, so you don't need yours.

facts.text: Each authorized employee must put a personal lock or tag on the group lockout device or group lockbox when starting work, and remove it when they stop working on the machine.
Group lockout gives one authorized employee primary responsibility for the employees working under the group lock.
Specific procedures must be used during shift or personnel changes to keep lockout protection in place, including an orderly transfer between off-going and oncoming employees.

story_seed: During a long repair, an off-going tech pulled their lock from the group box before the oncoming crew put theirs on. An oncoming mechanic was about to reach into the open guard when a coworker saw the empty box and stopped them.
crew_questions: How do we hand off a lockout here when a job runs past the end of a shift?
Who is in charge of the group lockbox on our big jobs, and how do we know everyone's lock is on?

title: Stored energy: springs, air, hydraulics
hazard: Energy can stay trapped in a machine after it is shut off and locked, and it can suddenly move parts, spray fluid or drop loads onto a worker.
key_points: Look for stored energy after you lock out: springs, air and hydraulic lines, raised parts, flywheels, and capacitors.
Bleed down, block, or restrain stored energy the way your site's procedure says.
Block raised parts so they cannot fall, and never rely on hydraulics alone to hold them up.
Keep checking during the job if pressure or energy could build back up.
Stop and ask if you cannot tell whether all energy is gone.
must_say: Locking the switch is not enough. Release or block the stored energy before you work.
never_say: Once the power is locked off, the machine is safe.
A hydraulic cylinder will hold a raised part up after shutdown.
Gauges reading zero mean you never need to check again.

facts.text: After locks or tags are applied, all hazardous stored or residual energy must be relieved, disconnected, restrained, or otherwise made safe.
If stored energy could build back up to a hazardous level, verification of isolation must continue until the work is done or the risk is gone.
Examples of stored energy listed in the standard include capacitors, springs, raised machine parts, rotating flywheels, hydraulic systems, and air, gas, steam or water pressure.

story_seed: A press was locked out at the disconnect, but nobody blocked the upper die. When a worker loosened a hydraulic fitting, the ram started to drift down and the worker pulled their hand back just in time.
crew_questions: Which machines in our area keep energy after they are shut off?
What blocks, pins or bleed valves do we have, and does everyone know where they are?

title: Prove it's dead: the try-out
hazard: A lock can be put on the wrong disconnect or a second energy source can be missed, so a machine that looks locked out can still start.
key_points: Make sure everyone is clear of the machine before the try-out.
Press the normal start button or controls to prove the machine will not run.
Have a qualified person test for voltage where your site's procedure calls for it. Never test for voltage unless you are qualified.
Put the controls back to off or neutral after the try-out.
Stop and report it if anything moves, hums or lights up.
must_say: Clear everyone, then try to start it before you touch it. If anything moves, stop and get help.
never_say: If the lock is on, you can skip the try-out.
A dark control panel proves the machine has no energy.
Leave the start button in the on position after testing.

facts.text: Before starting work on a locked or tagged out machine, the authorized employee must verify that isolation and de-energization have been done.
OSHA's sample procedure says to check that no one is exposed, then try the normal operating controls or test the equipment to make sure it will not operate, and then return the controls to off.

story_seed: A maintenance tech locked a breaker labeled for a conveyor and pressed start as a check. The conveyor jumped, because the label was wrong and the lock was on the next conveyor's breaker.
crew_questions: Do our machines have clear labels on every disconnect, and which ones are confusing?
What do we do if a try-out shows the machine still has power?

title: Machine guards stay on
hazard: Unguarded moving parts can grab, crush, cut or amputate fingers, hands and arms in an instant.
key_points: Check that every guard is in place and secure before you start a machine.
Stop and report a missing, loose or damaged guard right away.
Lock out before removing any guard for cleaning, adjusting or repair.
Put guards back before the machine runs again.
Use push sticks or hand tools only as extra protection, never instead of a guard.
must_say: If a guard is missing or damaged, do not run the machine. Tell your supervisor.
never_say: Experienced operators can run a machine without the guard.
A push stick replaces a guard.
Taking a guard off for a minute is fine if you are careful.

facts.text: Machine guarding must protect the operator and others in the area from hazards like the point of operation, ingoing nip points, rotating parts, and flying chips and sparks.
Guards must be attached to the machine where possible, and the guard itself must not create a hazard.
Special hand tools for placing material cannot take the place of required guarding; they can only add to it.

story_seed: An operator noticed a guard had been left off after a weekend repair. They almost started the machine to keep up with orders, but stopped and called maintenance first.
crew_questions: Which guard in our area gets taken off most often, and why?
What should you do if you find a guard missing at the start of your shift?

title: Never bypass an interlock
hazard: A bypassed interlock lets a machine run while a door or guard is open, so a person can reach into moving parts.
key_points: Never tape, tie, jumper or block an interlock switch or door sensor.
Report an interlock that is broken or keeps tripping instead of working around it.
Lock out the machine when you must go past a guard or safety device to clear, clean or fix it.
Tell your supervisor if you see a bypassed interlock, and stop the machine if it is safe to do so.
Follow your site's procedure for any approved service modes.
must_say: Never bypass an interlock. If it is in your way, stop and get it fixed.
never_say: It's OK to bypass an interlock if you're watching the machine.
Interlocks are just for new or untrained workers.
Using a spare key or magnet to cheat a door switch is a smart shortcut.

facts.text: Revolving drums, barrels and containers must be guarded by an enclosure that is interlocked with the drive so they cannot turn unless the guard is in place.
If a worker has to remove or bypass a guard or other safety device during servicing, the lockout/tagout standard applies.

story_seed: On a packaging line, someone wedged a zip tie into a door switch so the machine would keep running with the door open. A new worker reached in to fix a label and the arm cycled past their hand.
crew_questions: Are there interlocks here that trip so often that people are tempted to bypass them?
How do we report a bypassed or broken safety device on our line?

title: Pinch points and nip points
hazard: Hands and fingers can be caught and crushed where two parts come together, like rollers, belts, chains, gears and closing doors.
key_points: Spot the pinch points on your machine before you start work.
Keep hands, fingers and tools out of places where parts meet or close.
Keep guards in place over rollers, belts, chains and gears.
Lock out before reaching into a pinch point to clear or clean it.
Watch for pinch points when moving loads, closing doors or lowering parts.
must_say: Never reach into a pinch point while the machine can move.
never_say: You can pull your hand out in time if a roller grabs it.
Gloves protect your fingers in a nip point.
Pinch points are only on big machines.

facts.text: Machine guarding must protect workers from hazards such as ingoing nip points and rotating parts.

story_seed: A worker reached in to straighten film feeding into two rollers. Their glove tip got caught, and they pulled free only because a coworker hit the stop.
crew_questions: Where are the worst pinch points on our equipment?
What tasks tempt people to put a hand near moving rollers or chains?

title: Rotating parts: gloves, sleeves, hair, rings
hazard: Spinning shafts, chucks, drills and rollers can catch gloves, loose sleeves, long hair or jewelry and pull a person in.
key_points: Take off gloves before working near rotating parts.
Remove rings, watches, bracelets and necklaces before working near spinning parts.
Tie long hair back and tuck it under a cap, button or roll sleeves tight, and tuck in badge lanyards and loose strings.
Keep guards in place over shafts, couplings and spindles.
Never reach near a spinning part; stop the machine and wait until it stops turning before you brush chips, measure or adjust.
must_say: Near spinning parts, take gloves and jewelry off and tie long hair back.
never_say: A tighter or tougher glove makes it safe near a spinning shaft.
Wedding rings are fine because they are small.
A cap is not needed if your hair is only a little long.

facts.text: Machine guarding must protect workers from hazards such as rotating parts and ingoing nip points.

story_seed: A worker leaned over a lathe to brush away chips while wearing a loose glove. The chuck snagged the fingertip of the glove and pulled it before they could let go and step back.
crew_questions: Which machines here have spinning parts you can reach while they run?
What do we wear or carry that could get caught, and where do we store it during work?

title: Bench grinders
hazard: A grinder wheel can shatter and throw pieces, and a gap at the rest can pull work and fingers into the wheel.
key_points: Check the work rest and tongue guard gaps before you grind, with the grinder off.
Adjust the work rest and tongue guard only when the wheel is stopped.
Wear eye and face protection, and stand to the side when you start the grinder.
Let only trained people mount wheels; they inspect and ring test each wheel first. Never use a cracked or chipped wheel.
Never use a wheel whose marked speed is lower than the grinder's speed; report it instead.
Never grind on the side of a wheel unless it is made for that.
must_say: Adjust the rest and tongue only with the wheel stopped, and never use a cracked wheel.
never_say: A small gap at the work rest doesn't matter.
You can adjust the work rest while the wheel spins down.
Gloves make grinding small parts safe.

facts.text: On bench and other offhand grinders, the work rest must be kept within one-eighth inch of the wheel and must not be adjusted with the wheel moving.
The gap between the wheel and the adjustable tongue at the top of the guard must never be more than one-fourth inch.
Right before mounting, wheels must be inspected and ring tested, and the machine's spindle speed must not be higher than the speed marked on the wheel.

story_seed: A worker noticed the tool rest had worn far back from the wheel. A small part slipped into the gap and jerked their fingers toward the wheel before they let go.
crew_questions: Who checks the rest and tongue gaps on our grinders, and how often?
What do you do if a grinder wheel looks chipped or sounds wrong?

title: Working around conveyors
hazard: Conveyors can catch hands, clothes and hair in belts, rollers, chains and pulleys, and can pull a person in.
key_points: If someone gets caught, hit the nearest emergency stop or pull cord and shout for help. Know where they are and keep them clear.
Never climb on, ride on, or step over a running conveyor; use the crossover.
Keep guards on head and tail pulleys, drives and return rollers.
Lock out the conveyor before clearing jams, cleaning or fixing it.
Keep loose clothing, hair and gloves away from moving belts and rollers.
must_say: Never reach into, climb on or ride a running conveyor.
never_say: An emergency stop button is the same as lockout.
It's faster and fine to step over the conveyor.
You can clear a jam with the belt running if you are careful.

facts.text: Machine guarding must protect workers from hazards such as ingoing nip points and rotating parts.

story_seed: A worker tried to free a stuck box at the tail pulley while the belt was moving. Their sleeve got pulled toward the roller, and a coworker hit the pull cord.
crew_questions: Where are the e-stops and pull cords on our conveyors, and are any blocked?

title: Clearing jams safely
hazard: Jams tempt people to reach into a machine, and stuck parts or stored energy can suddenly release and cycle the machine.
key_points: Stop the machine and lock it out before reaching in to clear a jam.
Release or block stored energy, like air or springs, that can move parts when the jam frees.
Use only the clearing tool your site's procedure names for that machine, and only after it is locked out.
Never reach past a guard to clear a jam while the machine can move.
Report machines that jam often so the cause can be fixed.
must_say: Before you reach in to clear a jam, stop it and lock it out.
never_say: Small jams don't need lockout.
Just hit stop and reach in fast.
If the sensor is blocked, the machine can't start.

facts.text: Servicing during production is covered by lockout if a worker must remove or bypass a guard or place any part of the body in the point of operation or a danger zone.

story_seed: A case packer jammed and the operator reached in after pressing stop. When the jam freed, trapped air moved the pusher arm and it brushed their sleeve.
crew_questions: Which jams here happen the most, and how do we clear each one?
What would make it easier for us to lock out every time we clear a jam?

title: Robots and automated equipment
hazard: Robots and automated machines can move fast, start without warning, or pause and then start again, striking or crushing a person in their path.
key_points: Stay out of robot cells and fenced areas while the equipment can move.
Never step over a light curtain, open a gate, or defeat a sensor to get in.
Treat a paused or quiet robot as able to move at any time.
Lock out before entering for maintenance, cleaning or jam clearing, following your site's procedure.
Report any gate, door or sensor that does not stop the equipment.
must_say: A stopped robot can start again. Lock it out before you go in.
never_say: If the robot is not moving, it is safe to walk in.
You can reach past a light curtain if you are quick.
Robots always move the same way, so you can predict them.

facts.text: Point of operation guarding must keep the operator from having any part of the body in the danger zone during the operating cycle.
Servicing during production is covered by lockout if a worker must remove or bypass a guard or safety device, or place any part of the body in a danger zone.

story_seed: A technician stepped into a palletizer cell through an open gate because the robot looked stopped. It was only waiting for a sensor signal and swung toward the pallet as they reached it.
crew_questions: Which automated machines here could start up while a person is inside the guarded area?
How do we get into a robot cell safely for a jam or cleaning?

title: Inspect the ladder before you climb
hazard: A ladder with broken rungs, bent rails, missing feet or loose parts can fail and cause a fall.
key_points: Inspect the ladder before you use it on your shift.
Check rails, rungs, steps, feet, locks and spreaders for damage or missing parts.
Make sure rungs and feet are clean of oil, grease and mud.
Tag a damaged ladder 'Dangerous: Do Not Use' and take it out of service.
Never try to repair a damaged ladder yourself; follow your site's procedure.
must_say: If a ladder is damaged, tag it and take it out of service. Do not climb it.
never_say: A small crack in a rail is fine if you climb carefully.
Tape is a good fix for a broken rung.
You only need to inspect a ladder once a month.

facts.text: Ladders must be inspected before first use in each work shift, and more often as needed, for visible defects.
A ladder with structural or other defects must be tagged 'Dangerous: Do Not Use' or similar and removed from service until repaired or replaced.
Wooden ladders must not be coated with anything that could hide defects.

story_seed: A worker grabbed a stepladder that had been left in a corner. On the second step, a rivet popped on the spreader, and they stepped down before it folded.
crew_questions: Where do damaged ladders end up here, and how do we tag them?
What is the last thing you noticed wrong with a ladder at our site?

title: Setting up an extension ladder
hazard: An extension ladder that slides, tips or is set on a bad base can throw a worker to the ground.
key_points: Set the ladder on firm, level ground, and secure it on slippery surfaces.
Set the base out at the angle shown on the ladder's label.
Make sure both side rails rest on the top support.
Extend the rails at least 3 feet above the landing when you use it to get up to a level.
Face the ladder and keep one hand on it as you climb.
Barricade or secure ladders in doorways, aisles and traffic areas.
must_say: Never move, shift or extend a ladder while someone is on it.
never_say: You can lean a ladder on a box to get more height.
Tying two short ladders together works fine.
It's OK to scoot the ladder over while you're on it.

facts.text: Portable ladders used to reach an upper landing must have side rails that extend at least 3 feet above that landing.
A ladder must not be moved, shifted or extended while someone is on it.
Ladders must be used on stable, level surfaces unless secured, and must not be placed on boxes, barrels or other unstable bases.

story_seed: A worker set an extension ladder on a wet concrete floor without securing it. As they climbed, the feet began to slide out, and a coworker grabbed the base just in time.
crew_questions: Where do we use extension ladders here, and how do we secure them?
What should we do when the only spot for a ladder is in a busy aisle?

title: Stepladders and step stools
hazard: Stepladders that are not fully open, overloaded, or climbed too high can tip or fold and cause a fall.
key_points: Open the stepladder fully and lock the spreaders before you climb.
Never stand on the top cap or the top step.
Never use a closed stepladder leaned against a wall.
Face the ladder and keep at least one hand on it while climbing.
Keep tools and materials within your load rating, and don't carry loads that throw off your balance.
Use a taller ladder or a lift instead of overreaching.
must_say: Never stand on the top cap or top step of a stepladder.
never_say: The top cap is fine to stand on for a quick reach.
A folded stepladder is safe to lean against a wall.
Leaning out to one side is fine if you hold on.

facts.text: Each stepladder must have a metal spreader or locking device that holds the front and back open while it is in use.
The cap and top step of a stepladder must not be used as steps.
Workers must face the ladder and use at least one hand to grasp it when climbing up or down.

story_seed: A worker stood on the top step to reach a light fixture. The ladder rocked as they reached, and they caught the shelving to stop from falling.
crew_questions: Are our stepladders tall enough for the jobs we do?
Where are people tempted to stand on top of a stepladder or use a chair instead?

title: The 4-foot rule for edges
hazard: A fall from an open edge, platform or mezzanine can cause serious injury or death, even from a short height.
key_points: Stay back from any open edge that has no guardrail.
Use guardrails, nets or personal fall protection when working at an edge 4 feet or more above a lower level.
Never remove a guardrail or chain to make a job easier without your site's approved fall protection.
Put a removed guardrail or gate back before you leave the area.
Report missing guardrails, open gates and unmarked edges right away.
must_say: At an open edge 4 feet or more up, you need fall protection before you go near it.
never_say: Short falls can't hurt you.
Just be careful near the edge and you won't need protection.
A caution tape line is the same as a guardrail.

facts.text: Workers on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet or more above a lower level must be protected by guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall protection.

Workers 4 feet or more above dangerous equipment must be protected from falling, and workers less than 4 feet above it must be protected by guardrails or travel restraint unless the equipment is covered or guarded.

story_seed: A worker removed a mezzanine chain to lift a box up with a forklift. While waiting, they stepped back toward the open edge before a coworker called out.
crew_questions: Where are the open edges in our building, and are they all protected?
When do we take down a guardrail or gate here, and what protects us then?

title: Holes, skylights and covers
hazard: Workers can step into or fall through floor holes, openings, and skylights that are uncovered or have weak covers.
key_points: Never step, sit or lean on a skylight, even one with a screen, and never step on a cover you are not sure is secured.
Keep holes covered or guarded at all times, and secure covers so they cannot slide.
Put back any cover or guardrail you remove before you leave the area.
Report missing, loose or damaged covers right away.
Use guardrails or fall protection near skylights and open holes, following your site's procedure.
must_say: Never walk on a skylight or step on an unmarked cover.
never_say: Skylights are strong enough to walk on.
Plywood over a hole is always safe.
It's OK to leave a hole open for a few minutes.

facts.text: Workers must be protected from falling through any hole, including skylights, that is 4 feet or more above a lower level, by covers, guardrails, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest.
Workers must be protected from tripping or stepping into holes less than 4 feet above a lower level by covers or guardrails.
Each hole cover must hold at least twice the maximum intended load and be secured so it cannot be knocked out of place.

story_seed: A maintenance worker on a roof backed up while coiling a hose and stepped near a skylight. A coworker yelled just before their heel reached the plastic dome.
crew_questions: Where are the floor holes, hatches and skylights at our site?
How do we cover or guard a hole when we open one for work?

title: Guardrails
hazard: A missing, loose or damaged guardrail can let a worker fall from a platform, mezzanine, or edge.
key_points: Check that guardrails are in place and solid before you work near an edge.
Never sit on, stand on, climb, or lean hard on a guardrail.
Never use a guardrail as an anchor or to hoist materials.
Report loose, bent or missing rails right away and keep away from that edge.
Close gates and put back removed rails before you leave the area.
must_say: If a guardrail is missing or loose, stay back and report it.
never_say: You can lean on a guardrail to rest.
A chain or rope is just as strong as a guardrail.
It's fine to tie off your harness to any guardrail.

facts.text: The top rail of a guardrail must be 42 inches high, plus or minus 3 inches, above the walking-working surface.
Guardrails must withstand a force of at least 200 pounds applied downward or outward near the top edge.
Midrails, screens, or similar members are needed between the top rail and the walking surface when there is no wall or parapet at least 21 inches high.

story_seed: A worker on a mezzanine leaned against a section of guardrail that had been bumped by a forklift. The rail gave a few inches, and they stepped back from the edge.
crew_questions: Which guardrails here get bumped or removed most often?
How do we report a damaged guardrail, and who fixes it?

title: Fixed ladders and cages
hazard: Workers can fall from fixed ladders on tanks, roofs and mezzanines, especially when they slip, carry loads, or lose their grip.
key_points: Face the ladder and keep at least one hand on it while climbing.
Use the ladder safety system or fall arrest when the ladder has one.
Carry tools in a belt or hoist them up; keep your hands free.
Check rungs, rails, and the cage or safety system for damage before you climb.
Never count on a cage to catch you if you fall.
must_say: If the ladder has a safety system, connect to it before you climb.
never_say: A cage will stop your fall.
You can carry a bucket in one hand on a fixed ladder.
Fixed ladders don't need an inspection.

facts.text: Fixed ladders that extend more than 24 feet above a lower level need a personal fall arrest system, ladder safety system, cage or well if installed before November 19, 2018, and a personal fall arrest or ladder safety system if installed on or after that date.
By November 18, 2036, all fixed ladders over 24 feet must have a personal fall arrest or ladder safety system.
Workers must face the ladder, use at least one hand to grip it, and not carry anything that could make them lose balance.

story_seed: A worker climbed a caged ladder to a tank top carrying a toolbag in one hand. Their boot slipped on a wet rung, and they caught the rail with their free hand.
crew_questions: Which fixed ladders at our site have a ladder safety system, and which only have cages?
How do we get tools up a fixed ladder without carrying them?

title: Harness, lanyard and anchor checks
hazard: A damaged harness, wrong connector, or weak anchor can fail in a fall and let a worker hit the ground or a lower level.
key_points: If someone falls and is hanging in a harness, call 911 and start your site's rescue plan right away.
Inspect your harness, lanyard and connectors before use each shift.
Take any gear out of service if it is worn, cut, burned, mildewed, or has caught a fall.
Connect only to anchors your site has approved for fall arrest.
Wear the harness snug, with the back D-ring between your shoulder blades.
must_say: If your harness or lanyard has caught a fall or is damaged, take it out of service.
never_say: Any pipe or railing makes a good anchor.
A harness that has caught a fall is fine if it looks OK.
Body belts are fine for fall arrest.

facts.text: Personal fall protection must be inspected before first use during each work shift, and defective parts must be removed from service.
Gear that has been subjected to impact loading must be removed from service until a competent person says it is safe.
The employer must provide for prompt rescue of each employee in the event of a fall.

story_seed: Before going up in a boom lift, a worker checked their lanyard and found the shock pack partly torn open. They swapped it for new gear and reported the old one.
crew_questions: What anchors are approved for tie-off at our site?
If someone falls and is hanging in a harness here, what is our rescue plan?

title: Dock edges and dockboards
hazard: Workers and forklifts can fall from open dock edges, and trailers that creep or dockboards that shift can drop a load or a person.
key_points: Keep dock doors closed or guarded when no trailer is at the door.
Check that the trailer is chocked or locked to the dock before anyone goes on the dockboard.
Make sure the dockboard is secure and rated for the load.
Stay back from open dock edges, and never jump from the dock.
Follow your site's procedure for dock locks, lights and communication with drivers.
must_say: Never drive or walk onto a trailer until it is chocked or locked to the dock.
never_say: The driver will never pull away while you're loading.
A dockboard will stay in place on its own.
It's faster and fine to jump down from the dock.

facts.text: Wheel chocks, sand shoes or similar measures must be used to keep the truck, trailer or rail car from moving while workers are on the dockboard.
Portable dockboards must be anchored or secured so they cannot move out of a safe position.
Workers on a dockboard must be protected from falling 4 feet or more by a guardrail or handrails, with limited exceptions for some material handling with motorized equipment.

story_seed: A forklift driver started into a trailer when the truck began to roll forward. The dockboard dropped a few inches and the driver stopped and backed out.
crew_questions: How do we know a trailer is chocked or locked before we go in?
Where are open dock edges left unguarded at our site?

title: Scissor lifts and aerial lifts
hazard: Workers can fall from, be thrown from, or be crushed by lifts that tip over, hit overhead objects, or move unexpectedly.
key_points: Test the lift controls and inspect the lift before use each day.
Only operate a lift you are trained on.
Stand on the platform floor; never climb or stand on the rails or use a ladder in the basket.
In a boom lift, wear a harness and tie off to the boom or basket anchor.
Stay well away from overhead power lines, and follow your site's procedure for minimum distances.
Check the ground for holes, slopes and drop-offs before you raise or drive.
must_say: Never climb on the rails or use a ladder in a lift basket.
never_say: You can tie off to a nearby beam from a boom lift.
Leaning over the rail is fine if your harness is on.
Driving a raised lift is fine on any floor.

facts.text: For vehicle-mounted boom lifts, lift controls must be tested each day before use.
Workers in vehicle-mounted boom lifts must stand firmly on the basket floor, not sit or climb on the edge, and not use planks or ladders to work from.
Workers in these boom lifts must wear a personal fall arrest or travel restraint system attached to the boom or basket, and must not tie off to a nearby pole or structure.

story_seed: A worker in a scissor lift drove it while raised and didn't see a floor drain cover was missing. The wheel dipped, the platform swayed, and they lowered it right away.
crew_questions: What do we check on our lifts before each use?
Where at our site are there overhead hazards or floor drop-offs near lift work?

title: Slips, trips and falls on the level
hazard: Wet floors, clutter, cords and uneven surfaces can cause slips and trips that lead to falls and serious injuries.
key_points: Keep aisles, walkways and exits clear of boxes, hoses, cords and tools.
Guard and report spills as soon as you see them, and clean them up only if you know they are safe to handle.
Wear the slip-resistant shoes your site requires.
Walk, don't run, and watch where you step, especially when carrying loads.
Report loose mats, damaged flooring and poor lighting.
must_say: If you see a spill or trip hazard, guard it and report it. Never walk past it.
never_say: Slips are just bad luck and can't be prevented.
It's someone else's job to pick up clutter.
Walking faster gets you past a wet spot safely.

facts.text: Workplaces, passageways and walking-working surfaces must be kept clean, orderly and sanitary.
Floors must be kept clean and, as far as feasible, dry; where wet processes are used, drainage must be maintained and dry standing places like mats or platforms provided where feasible.

story_seed: A worker carrying a box couldn't see a strapping band on the floor. Their foot caught it, and they stumbled before catching the rack.
crew_questions: Where do slips and trips happen most at our site?
What is one cleanup habit our crew could do better?

title: Clean it up or guard it
hazard: Spills and leaks on floors can cause slips and falls, and some spills can also burn skin or give off harmful vapors.
key_points: If a spill is a chemical, unknown, large, or gives off fumes, move away, keep others back, and tell your supervisor right away.
Guard any spill you can safely stand near so no one walks through it.
Clean it up yourself only if you know what it is and are trained; follow your site's spill procedure.
Find and report the source of leaks so they get fixed.
Put up a cone or sign until the floor is dry.
must_say: If you can't clean it up right now, guard it so no one walks through it.
never_say: A wet floor sign means the spill is cleaned up.
Any spill can be wiped up with paper towels.
Leaks that come back every day are normal.

facts.text: Walking-working surfaces must be kept free of hazards such as leaks, spills, snow and ice.
Hazardous conditions must be fixed before anyone uses the surface again; if that can't happen right away, the hazard must be guarded to keep people off it.

story_seed: A forklift was leaking hydraulic oil near a doorway. A worker stepped in the puddle and slipped, but caught the door frame, and then placed cones and reported it.
crew_questions: Where are our spill kits and wet floor signs?
Which leaks around here keep coming back, and who do we tell?

title: Ice and snow on walkways
hazard: Ice, snow and slush on walkways, docks and entrances can cause hard falls, and wet tracked-in water makes indoor floors slippery.
key_points: Walk slowly with short steps on icy surfaces, and keep your hands free.
Use handrails and the cleared, treated paths.
Wear footwear with good grip, and use ice cleats if your site provides them.
Report icy spots, drips and snow buildup at doors and docks.
Wipe feet and watch for wet floors just inside entrances.
must_say: Report ice right away, and take the cleared path even if it is longer.
never_say: Ice is only dangerous when it looks shiny.
Hands in pockets keep you warm and steady.
Shortcuts over snowbanks are fine.

facts.text: Walking-working surfaces must be kept free of hazards such as snow and ice.
Hazardous walking surfaces must be fixed before use, or guarded to keep workers off until they are fixed.

story_seed: On an early shift, a worker started to cut across the parking lot instead of using the salted walk. Their foot slid on black ice, and they grabbed a car mirror, then went back to the cleared path.
crew_questions: Where does ice or snow build up first at our site?
Who do we call when a walkway or dock needs salt or plowing?

title: Stairs and handrails
hazard: Missing a step, carrying loads that block your view, or not holding the rail can lead to falls on stairs.
key_points: Use the handrail every time you go up or down.
Keep one hand free for the rail; get help with large or heavy loads.
Watch your step and don't use your phone on stairs.
Keep stairs clear of boxes, tools and spills.
Report loose rails, damaged treads and poor lighting.
must_say: Hold the handrail on every stairway, every time.
never_say: Handrails are only for older workers.
You can carry boxes on stairs as long as you can see over them.
Running on stairs is fine when you're in a hurry.

facts.text: Each flight of stairs with at least 3 treads and at least 4 risers must have stair rail systems and handrails.
Handrails must withstand a force of at least 200 pounds applied downward or outward.
Stairs must have uniform riser heights and tread depths between landings.

story_seed: A worker carried two cases down a stairway, so they couldn't see the steps or hold the rail. They missed the bottom step and caught themselves on the wall.
crew_questions: Which stairs at our site are hard to use safely, and why?
How do we move materials between floors without carrying them on stairs?

title: Housekeeping that prevents injuries
hazard: Spills, clutter, and loose material on floors and in aisles cause slips, trips, and falls, and can block exits and emergency equipment.
key_points: Clean up a small spill right away only if you know what it is and it is safe; otherwise block it off and report it.
Keep aisles, walkways, and exits clear of pallets, hoses, cords, and scrap.
Put tools and materials back where they belong when you finish with them.
Report loose boards, holes, leaks, and damaged floors so they get fixed.
Keep the space in front of fire extinguishers, eyewash stations, and electrical panels clear.
Never walk past a hazard you could safely fix or report.
must_say: If you see a spill, block it off and report it. Clean it only if you know it is safe.
never_say: Housekeeping is the cleaning crew's job, not yours.
A small spill can wait until the end of the shift.
It's fine to leave things in an aisle for a little while.

facts.text: Workplaces, passageways, and storerooms must be kept clean and orderly. Walking surfaces must be kept free of hazards like sharp or sticking-out objects, loose boards, leaks, and spills.
Floors must be kept clean and, as far as possible, dry. Where wet processes are used, drains must be kept working and dry places to stand, like mats or platforms, provided where possible.
A hazard on a walking surface must be fixed before anyone uses that surface again. If it cannot be fixed right away, it must be guarded so no one uses it.

story_seed: A worker carrying a box down an aisle stepped on a strip of shrink wrap lying on a wet spot and caught themselves on a rack. The wrap had been there since the shift before.
crew_questions: Where on our floor do spills or clutter show up most, and why?
What gets in the way of keeping our aisles and exits clear?

title: Forklift pre-shift check
hazard: A forklift with bad brakes, steering, forks, horn, or a leak can lose control, drop a load, or hit someone.
key_points: Check the forklift before you use it each shift, using your site's checklist.
Look at the forks, chains, mast, tires, and overhead guard for cracks, damage, or wear.
Test the brakes, steering, horn, lights, and backup alarm before you move a load.
Look for leaks of oil, fuel, hydraulic fluid, or battery acid under and around the truck.
Tag the forklift out of service and tell your supervisor if anything is wrong.
Never drive a forklift with a fuel leak or any problem that affects safe use.
must_say: If the check finds a problem, the forklift does not run. Tag it out and report it.
never_say: If you're running late, you can skip the check this one time.
A small hydraulic leak is fine as long as the forks still lift.
Only maintenance needs to look the truck over.

facts.text: Forklifts must be examined before being placed in service, at least daily. Where they are used around the clock, they must be examined after each shift. Defects must be reported right away and corrected.
A forklift that needs repair, is defective, or is unsafe in any way must be taken out of service until it is fixed.
No truck may be operated with a leak in the fuel system until the leak is fixed.

story_seed: During a pre-shift check, an operator found the horn did not work and a hydraulic hose was weeping fluid. They tagged the truck out, and the hose later split on the repair stand instead of under a raised load.
crew_questions: What problems have our pre-shift checks caught lately?
What makes it hard to do a full check at the start of a shift here?

title: Forklift training and evaluation
hazard: Untrained or out-of-practice drivers can tip a forklift, drop a load, or strike someone on foot.
key_points: Never drive a forklift until you are trained, evaluated, and authorized by your site.
Drive only the types of trucks and attachments you were trained and evaluated on.
Speak up if you are asked to drive a truck you have not been trained on.
Ask for refresher training when you get a new truck type or attachment, or when your work area changes.
Follow what your training taught about this site's ramps, aisles, loads, and walkways.
must_say: If you have not been trained and evaluated on that truck, do not drive it.
never_say: If you can drive a car, you can drive a forklift.
Training on one kind of truck means you can drive any truck here.
A quick lap around the lot counts as training.

facts.text: Before anyone drives a forklift on the job, they must complete training and an evaluation. Trainees may drive only under direct supervision of a qualified trainer, and only where it does not put anyone in danger.
Refresher training is required in several cases, including when an operator is assigned to a different type of truck or a change in the workplace affects safe driving.
Each operator's driving must be evaluated at least once every three years.

story_seed: A new hire was asked to "just move one pallet" with a stand-up reach truck they had never driven. They said they were not trained on it, and a trained operator moved it instead.
crew_questions: Which trucks or attachments here are you trained on, and which are you not?
What should someone do here if they are asked to drive something they are not trained on?

title: Parking a forklift
hazard: A forklift left with raised forks, power on, or brakes off can roll, be bumped into, or trip and strike people walking by.
key_points: Fully lower the forks to the floor every time you get off the truck.
Put the controls in neutral and set the brake before you step off.
Shut off the power when you walk away or lose sight of the truck.
Block the wheels if you must park on a slope.
Park only in approved spots, never in aisles, exits, or in front of fire equipment or stairways.
Follow your site's rules for keys so no one untrained can drive it.
must_say: Every time you leave the truck: forks down, controls in neutral, brake set.
never_say: It's fine to leave the forks up if you'll be right back.
Parking in the aisle is fine for a quick break.
You can leave it running while you step away.

facts.text: A forklift is unattended when the operator is 25 ft or more away, or cannot see it. Then the forks must be fully lowered, controls put in neutral, power shut off, and brakes set. Wheels must be blocked on an incline.
When the operator is off the truck but within 25 ft and can still see it, the forks must be fully lowered, controls put in neutral, and brakes set.
Fire aisles, access to stairways, and fire equipment must be kept clear.

story_seed: An operator hopped off to grab paperwork and left the forks raised at chest height in a walkway. A coworker carrying a box around the end of a rack nearly walked into the fork tips.
crew_questions: Where do people tend to park forklifts here when they are in a hurry?
Do we have enough marked parking spots, and are they in the right places?

title: Pedestrians and forklifts
hazard: Forklifts are heavy, can be quiet, and are hard to see around, so people on foot can be struck, pinned, or crushed.
key_points: Walk only in marked walkways, and cross aisles at marked crossings where your site has them.
Stop and make eye contact with the driver before you cross in front of a forklift.
Never walk or stand under raised forks, loaded or empty.
Drivers: slow down and sound the horn at cross aisles, doorways, and blind corners.
Drivers: travel with the load trailing when it blocks your view ahead.
Never ride on a forklift unless there is a safe place to ride and you are authorized.
must_say: Never walk or stand under raised forks.
Make eye contact with the driver before you cross in front of a forklift.
never_say: Pedestrians always have the right of way, so forklifts will stop for you.
A backup alarm means the driver sees you.
Wearing a bright vest means drivers will always see you.

facts.text: No one may stand or pass under the raised part of any truck, loaded or empty.
Drivers must slow down and sound the horn at cross aisles and other places where they cannot see. If the load blocks the view ahead, they must travel with the load trailing.
Trucks must not be driven up to anyone standing in front of a bench or other fixed object.

story_seed: A worker stepped out from between two racks while reading a pick list just as a forklift came around the end of the aisle. The driver had slowed and sounded the horn, and both stopped in time.
crew_questions: Where on our site do people on foot and forklifts cross paths the most?
What blind spots or shortcuts do you see people use here?

title: Forklift loads and tip-overs
hazard: Overloaded, off-balance, or raised loads can make a forklift tip over or drop a load, and a tip-over can crush the driver.
key_points: Check the capacity plate and never lift more than the truck is rated for.
Carry loads low, tilted back, and only high enough to clear the floor.
On ramps and slopes, keep the load on the uphill side.
Slow down for turns and turn the wheel smoothly.
Tilt a raised load forward only when it is over the rack or stack where you are setting it down.
On a sit-down truck, wear your seatbelt; if it tips, never jump: stay in, hold on, lean away. Stand-up trucks: follow your training.
must_say: If a sit-down forklift starts to tip, do not jump. Stay in, hold on, and lean away.
never_say: If the forklift starts to tip, jump clear.
Every kind of forklift uses the same move to escape a tip-over.
Carrying the load high helps you see under it.

facts.text: Only stable or safely arranged loads, within the truck's rated capacity, may be handled. Use caution with off-center loads that cannot be centered.
On grades over 10 percent, loaded trucks must be driven with the load upgrade. On all grades, the load must be tilted back if possible and raised only enough to clear the road surface.
Tilting forward with the forks raised is not allowed except to pick up a load. A raised load may be tilted forward only when it is in place over a rack or stack.

story_seed: An operator picked up a pallet of mixed parts that was heavier on one side and started up the dock ramp with the load raised to see over it. The back of the truck felt light, so they stopped, lowered the load, and had it restacked.
crew_questions: Which loads here are hardest to keep stable, and why?
Where are the ramps, slopes, or rough floors that make tip-overs more likely?

title: Battery charging and propane changes
hazard: Charging batteries give off flammable gas and contain acid that burns skin and eyes, and leaking propane can catch fire or explode.
key_points: If acid hits your eyes or skin, flush at the eyewash or shower now, call for help, and keep flushing until help says stop.
If you smell propane or hear a hiss, move away, keep others back, do not start or switch anything on, and report it.
Charge batteries or change propane tanks only if you are trained, and follow your site's procedure.
Park in the charging or fueling area, set the brake, and shut the truck off before you start.
Never smoke, use open flames, or make sparks near charging batteries or propane, and keep tools off battery tops.
Wear the eye, face, and hand protection your site requires for this job.
must_say: No smoking, flames, or sparks near charging batteries or propane.
Shut the truck off and set the brake before charging or changing fuel.
never_say: You can charge a forklift battery anywhere there is an outlet.
Pour water into acid to dilute it.
It's fine to change a propane tank with the engine running.

facts.text: Battery charging must be done in areas set aside for it, with ways to flush and neutralize spilled battery acid, fire protection, and enough ventilation to clear battery fumes.
Smoking is banned in the charging area, open flames, sparks, and electric arcs must be prevented, and tools and other metal objects must be kept off the top of uncovered batteries.
The truck must be in position with the brake set before changing or charging batteries. Fuel tanks must not be filled while the engine is running.

story_seed: An operator about to swap a propane tank noticed a hissing sound and frost forming at the valve on the new tank. They stopped, moved away, kept others back, and called their supervisor.
crew_questions: Where are our charging and fueling areas, and what do we keep near them that should not be there?
Where is the nearest eyewash to the charging area, and does it work?

title: Pallet jacks
hazard: Pallet jacks can crush feet, pin people against racks, walls, or trailers, and strain backs and shoulders when loads are heavy.
key_points: Check the jack before use: wheels, handle, forks, brakes, and controls. Tag out and report anything broken.
Keep your feet and other people clear of the wheels and forks.
Use a powered pallet jack only if you are trained and authorized to use it.
Go slow at corners, doorways, and blind spots, and follow your site's rules for ramps and dock plates.
Never ride on a walk-behind pallet jack or use it to carry people.
Lower the forks fully and park the jack out of walkways when you are done.
must_say: Keep your feet and other people clear of the wheels and forks.
never_say: Riding on a walk-behind pallet jack is fine if you go slow.
Anyone can use a powered pallet jack without training.
You can move any load with a pallet jack if you go slowly.
story_seed: A worker backing a powered pallet jack out of a trailer felt their heel come close to the drive wheel near the trailer wall. They let go of the control, stopped, and changed their position before moving again.
crew_questions: Where do pallet jacks and people get squeezed into tight spaces here?
What loads do we move by pallet jack that are really too heavy or awkward for it?

title: Lifting without hurting your back
hazard: Lifting, twisting, and carrying loads the wrong way strains backs, shoulders, and knees, and the damage can build up over time.
key_points: Size up the load first: test the weight, check for sharp edges, and plan your path.
Use a cart, hoist, lift table, or pallet jack when one is available.
Get close to the load, bend your knees, keep your back straight, and lift with your legs.
Keep the load close to your body and between your shoulders and knees when you can.
Turn with your feet instead of twisting your back.
Report pain or numbness early, before it becomes a bigger injury.
must_say: If a load is too heavy or awkward, stop and get help or a lifting aid.
never_say: If you lift with your legs, any weight is safe.
A back belt lets you lift more safely.
Pain is normal, just push through it.
story_seed: A worker reached deep into a bin to pull out a heavy box and felt a twinge in their lower back. They stopped, asked a coworker to help tip the bin, and reported the twinge to their supervisor.
crew_questions: Which lifts here feel the hardest on your body?
Where could a cart, lift table, or other aid make a lift easier?

title: Team lifts and asking for help
hazard: Loads that are too heavy, long, or awkward for one person cause strains, dropped loads, and crushed hands and feet, and a team lift without a plan can go wrong fast.
key_points: Ask for help before you lift something too heavy, long, or awkward for one person.
Pick one person to call the lift, and agree on the plan and path before you start.
Clear the path and check for doors, steps, and tight spots first.
Lift, move, and set down together on the leader's count.
Say "stop" if anyone loses grip or footing, and set the load down together.
Use a cart, hoist, or other lifting aid instead of a team lift when one is available.
must_say: If a load is too much for you, stop and ask for help.
One person calls the lift, and everyone moves together.
never_say: Asking for help slows the job down, so just do it yourself.
On a team lift, everyone can lift when they're ready.
Adding more people makes any load safe.
story_seed: Two workers carrying a long steel panel reached a doorway, and one turned without warning. The other felt the panel pull and called "stop", and they set it down and planned the turn before going on.
crew_questions: What loads here should always be team lifts or use a lifting aid?
What makes people here not ask for help, and how can we change that?

title: Stacking and storage
hazard: Unstable stacks and overloaded or damaged racks can collapse or drop items onto people, and storage in aisles causes trips and blocks exits.
key_points: If a stack or rack starts to lean or fall, get clear, warn others, and never try to catch it.
Stack heavy items low and lighter items higher, and keep stacks square and stable.
Never load a rack or shelf beyond its marked capacity or above the height your site allows.
Never climb racks or shelves; use an approved ladder or lift.
Report damaged racks, bent uprights, or leaning stacks, and keep people away from them.
Keep aisles, exits, and fire equipment clear of stored materials.
must_say: Report a damaged rack or leaning stack and keep people away from it.
never_say: If a stack leans a little, just push it back into place.
Climbing a rack is fine for a quick grab.
It's fine to use an aisle for extra storage for a day.

facts.text: Materials stored in tiers must be stacked, blocked, interlocked, and limited in height so they are stable and won't slide or collapse.
Aisles and passageways must be kept clear and in good repair, with nothing in or across them that could create a hazard.
Storage areas must be kept free of piled-up materials that create trip, fire, explosion, or pest hazards.

story_seed: A worker noticed a rack upright had been bent by a forklift and the shelf above was sagging under a full pallet. They roped off the bay and reported it before anyone pulled stock from it.
crew_questions: Where do stacks or racks look unstable or damaged here?
Where does stored material creep into aisles or in front of exits?

title: Overhead crane basics
hazard: A dropped, swinging, or overloaded crane load can crush or strike people, and a failed hook, chain, or rope can let a load fall without warning.
key_points: Run a crane only if you are trained and designated to operate it.
Check the crane before use with your site's checklist, and report damaged hooks, chains, ropes, or controls.
Know the load's weight and never lift more than the crane's marked rated load.
Lift the load just a few inches first to check balance and rigging before going higher.
Never carry a load over people; sound the warning and wait for the path to clear.
Never leave the controls while a load is hanging.
must_say: Never carry a load over people, and never leave the controls with a load hanging.
never_say: It's fine to move a load over people if you go slow.
The upper limit switch can be used as a normal stop.
Anyone who has watched it done can run the crane.

facts.text: Only designated people may operate a crane.
A crane must not be loaded beyond its rated load, and the rated load must be marked on each side of the crane so it can be read from the floor.
The operator must avoid carrying loads over people, must sound the warning signal when the load or hook nears or goes over people, and must not leave the controls while a load is hanging.

story_seed: A crane operator was moving a die across the bay when a worker stepped into the path from behind a machine. The operator stopped, sounded the warning, and waited for the worker to clear before moving on.
crew_questions: Where do crane loads travel near where people work or walk here?
What problems have come up in our crane checks, and were they fixed?

title: Slings and rigging
hazard: A damaged, overloaded, or badly rigged sling can break or slip and drop the load, and hands can be crushed between a sling and the load.
key_points: Inspect slings and hardware before each use, and take damaged ones out of service.
Never use a sling with a missing or unreadable tag.
Never tie knots in a sling or shorten it with bolts or other makeshift fixes.
Pad slings where they wrap around sharp edges.
Keep hands and fingers out from between the sling and the load as it tightens.
Never pull a sling out from under a load that is resting on it.
must_say: If a sling is damaged or has no readable tag, do not use it.
never_say: A knot is a fine way to shorten a sling.
A small cut in a web sling is okay if the load is light.
You can guide the load by holding the sling as it tightens.

facts.text: Each day before use, slings and all fastenings and attachments must be inspected for damage by a competent person chosen by the employer. Damaged or defective slings must be removed from service right away.
Slings must not be shortened with knots, bolts, or other makeshift devices, and must not be loaded beyond their rated capacity.
Slings without attached, readable identification markings must not be used.

story_seed: While rigging a motor for a lift, a worker found a web sling with a cut edge and a worn-off tag. They set it aside, tagged it out, and got a good sling from the rigging rack.
crew_questions: Where do we keep slings here, and how do damaged ones get taken out of use?
Which of our loads have sharp edges that need padding?

title: Never under a suspended load
hazard: A load hanging from a crane or hoist can fall, swing, or shift at any moment and crush anyone under it or in its path.
key_points: Never walk or stand under a suspended load, even for a moment.
Stay out of the path the load will travel and out of the area where it could fall or swing.
Stop the lift and warn people if anyone walks into the lift area.
Never ride on a load or a hook.
Guide loads the way your site's procedure says, such as with a tag line, and keep your body out of pinch points.
Keep barricades and lift zones in place until the load is set down.
must_say: Never walk or stand under a suspended load.
never_say: It's okay to pass under a load if you're quick.
If you know where the load is going, you can stand close to it.
Riding the hook is fine for a short move.

facts.text: All employees must be kept clear of loads about to be lifted and of suspended loads.
The crane operator must avoid carrying loads over people.
While anyone is on the load or hook, there must be no hoisting, lowering, or traveling.

story_seed: A worker took a shortcut across the bay while a crane was moving a steel coil overhead. A coworker shouted, the operator stopped, and the worker backed out before the load passed over.
crew_questions: Where are the lift paths in our area, and how do people know when a lift is happening?
When do people here feel pushed to take a shortcut under or near a load?

title: Keep electrical panels clear
hazard: Blocked or damaged electrical panels slow down shutting off power in an emergency and can expose people to shock, burns, and arc flash.
key_points: If a panel is smoking, sparking, or smells like burning, stay back, keep others away, and call for help.
Keep the floor space in front of electrical panels clear of carts, pallets, boxes, and trash.
Never store or stack anything in front of or against a panel, even for a short time.
Keep panel doors closed and report missing covers or open holes.
Report breaker and disconnect labels that are missing or hard to read.
Never reset a breaker that keeps tripping; report it to a qualified person.
must_say: Keep the space in front of every electrical panel clear, all the time.
never_say: It's fine to park a cart in front of a panel for a little while.
If a breaker trips, keep resetting it until it holds.
A missing panel cover is fine if you're careful.

facts.text: The working space in front of electrical equipment may not be used for storage.
The working space in front of electrical equipment must be at least as wide as the equipment or 30 inches, whichever is more, and must let equipment doors open at least 90 degrees.
Each disconnect and circuit must be clearly marked to show what it is for, unless its purpose is obvious.

story_seed: During a power problem, a maintenance tech had to move a stack of boxed parts before reaching the panel to shut off a machine. The parts had been put there "just for the day" a week earlier.
crew_questions: Which panels in our area get blocked most often, and by what?
Can you find and reach the disconnect for the machine you run?

title: Extension cords
hazard: Damaged or misused extension cords can shock people, start fires, and cause trips.
key_points: Check each cord before use for cuts, crushed spots, missing ground pins, and loose plugs.
Take damaged cords out of service; never tape over a cut or broken jacket.
Never run cords through doorways, windows, or holes in walls, or use them as permanent wiring.
Keep cords out of walkways and traffic, or protect them so they are not run over or tripped on.
Use a cord rated for the job and the location, including outdoor or wet areas.
Never remove a ground pin or use an adapter that breaks the ground.
must_say: If a cord is cut, crushed, or missing a ground pin, take it out of service.
never_say: Electrical tape makes a damaged cord safe again.
It's fine to cut off the ground pin to fit an old outlet.
Extension cords can be used as permanent wiring if they're taped down.

facts.text: Flexible cords may not be used in place of permanent building wiring, run through holes in walls, ceilings, or floors, run through doorways or windows, attached to building surfaces, or hidden behind walls, ceilings, or floors.
Cords must be connected to devices and fittings with strain relief, so a pull on the cord does not pull directly on joints or terminal screws.
Extension cords must be visually inspected before use on any shift for loose parts, bent or missing pins, damage to the outer jacket, and signs of inside damage like pinched or crushed spots.

story_seed: A worker found an extension cord running under a closed door to power a fan, with the jacket crushed flat where the door pinched it. They unplugged it, tagged it out, and asked maintenance about a proper outlet.
crew_questions: Where do we use extension cords here that should really be permanent outlets?
Where do cords cross walkways or get run over?

title: Qualified and unqualified: who touches live parts
hazard: Touching or getting too close to live electrical parts can cause shock, burns, and death, and untrained workers may not see the danger.
key_points: If someone is being shocked, do not touch them; shut off the power if you safely can and call 911.
Never open electrical panels or work on live parts unless you are trained and authorized as a qualified person.
Never bypass or defeat an electrical interlock or guard.
Never reach blindly into a space that might have live parts.
Stay out of areas marked with barricades or signs for electrical work.
Treat wires and parts as live until a qualified person says otherwise, and report problems to them.
must_say: If you are not qualified, do not touch it. Call a qualified person.
If someone is being shocked, do not touch them. Shut off power if you can and call 911.
never_say: Low voltage can't hurt you, so anyone can work on it.
If you've done wiring at home, you can do it here.
You can pull a person off a live wire if you're quick.

facts.text: Only qualified persons may work on electrical parts or equipment that have not been deenergized and locked out or tagged.
Qualified persons must be trained to tell exposed live parts from other parts, to find the voltage of live parts, and to know the required clearance distances.
Only a qualified person following energized-work rules may defeat an electrical safety interlock, and only for the time they are working on the equipment.

story_seed: A machine stopped mid-shift and an operator reached for the control cabinet door to "just check a fuse." A coworker stopped them, and they called the on-shift electrician instead.
crew_questions: Who are the qualified electrical people on our shift, and how do we reach them?
Where are people tempted to open a panel or bypass an interlock to keep running?

title: Damaged cords and power tools
hazard: A damaged cord or power tool can shock or burn the user, start a fire, or fail in a way that injures the user.
key_points: If a tool shocks you, sparks, or smokes, stop, unplug it if it is safe to, and report it.
Look over every cord and power tool before you use it each shift.
Tag out any cord or tool with cuts, crushed spots, bent or missing pins, cracked housings, or loose parts.
Never lift, lower, or drag a tool by its cord.
Never staple cords or hang them in a way that could damage them.
Never use a tool with its ground pin removed or its guard missing.
must_say: If a cord or tool is damaged, tag it out and do not use it.
never_say: Tape fixes a cut cord.
A small tingle from a tool is normal.
You can carry a drill by its cord.

facts.text: Cord-and-plug tools and extension cords must be visually inspected before use on any shift for loose parts, bent or missing pins, damage to the outer jacket, and signs of inside damage like pinched or crushed spots.
If a cord or tool has a defect that could hurt someone, it must be removed from service and no one may use it until it is repaired and tested.
Cords may not be used to raise or lower equipment, and may not be stapled or hung in a way that could damage the jacket or insulation.

story_seed: A worker picked up a grinder and noticed the cord jacket was split near the handle with the inner wires showing. They tagged it out and got another grinder from the tool crib.
crew_questions: How do damaged tools get tagged out and replaced here?
Which tools or cords in our area get beat up the most, and why?

title: Electricity and water
hazard: Water lets electricity flow through your body much more easily, so wet floors, wet hands, and wet equipment greatly raise the risk of serious shock.
key_points: If someone is shocked near water, do not touch them or step into the water; shut off power if you safely can and call 911.
Keep cords, plugs, and tools out of water and off wet floors.
Dry your hands before you plug in or unplug anything.
Use only tools and cords approved for wet areas, plugged into ground-fault protection (GFCI) as your site's procedure says.
Report water near panels, outlets, or machines, and lock out equipment before washdown as your site's procedure says.
Stop using any tool or cord that gets wet and have it checked before using it again.
must_say: Never plug in or unplug anything with wet hands.
never_say: Rubber boots make it safe to work with electricity in water.
A tool that got wet is fine once it looks dry.
It's okay to hose down a machine's control panel while it's running.

facts.text: Unless they are identified for use there, electrical wiring and equipment may not be located in damp or wet locations.
Portable tools and cords used where workers are likely to contact water or other conductive liquids must be approved for those locations.
Hands may not be wet when plugging and unplugging energized cords and equipment.

story_seed: During a washdown, a worker noticed a portable fan plugged into an outlet near the floor with water pooling around the cord. They stopped spraying, had the circuit shut off, and moved the fan once power was off.
crew_questions: Where in our area do water and electricity come close together?
What is our site's procedure for washdown around electrical equipment?

title: Arc flash awareness
hazard: An arc flash is an electrical explosion that can cause severe burns, blindness, hearing damage, and blast injuries in a split second.
key_points: If an arc flash happens, call 911, keep others back, and do not touch anyone who may still be in contact with equipment.
Stay out of marked electrical work areas and behind barricades unless you are qualified and authorized.
Never open a panel or work on live equipment unless you are qualified, authorized, and wearing the protective gear (PPE) your site requires.
Ask for equipment to be shut off and locked out before work near live parts.
Remove rings, watches, and other metal jewelry before any electrical work.
Report panels that buzz, smell hot, or show burn marks, and keep people away.
must_say: If you are not qualified and authorized, stay back from open electrical equipment.
never_say: Regular work clothes and safety glasses are enough for any electrical work.
Arc flash only happens on high-voltage power lines.
You're safe from arc flash as long as you don't touch anything.

facts.text: Live parts must be deenergized before an employee works on or near them, unless the employer can show that deenergizing creates greater hazards or is not possible.
Employees must wear eye or face protection wherever there is danger from electric arcs or flashes, or from objects thrown by an electrical explosion.
Conductive jewelry and clothing, like rings, watch bands, and key chains, may not be worn if they might contact exposed live parts, unless they are made nonconductive.

story_seed: A panel cover was off for troubleshooting and a worker walked up to watch over the electrician's shoulder. The electrician stopped and asked them to stay behind the barricade until the work was done.
crew_questions: Which panels or equipment here are opened most often while live?
How do we mark off an area when electrical work is going on?

title: Why your protective gear (PPE) was chosen
hazard: Wearing the wrong protective gear, damaged gear, or no gear leaves workers open to the hazards the gear was picked to stop.
key_points: Wear the protective gear (PPE) your task requires, every time, for the whole task.
Ask your supervisor what hazard each piece of gear protects you from.
Check your gear before each use and replace it if it is damaged or worn out.
Tell your supervisor if your gear doesn't fit or gets in the way of the job.
Speak up when a job, chemical, or machine changes so the gear choice can be checked again.
Use guards, lockout, and other controls first; gear is the last line of defense.
must_say: If your gear is damaged or does not fit, do not use it. Get a replacement.
never_say: Any gloves will do for any job.
If you wear protective gear, you don't need machine guards.
Damaged gear is better than no gear.

facts.text: The employer must check the workplace for hazards that call for protective gear, pick gear that protects against them, tell each affected worker what was picked, and choose gear that fits each worker.
Defective or damaged protective gear must not be used.

Workers must be trained on when gear is needed, what gear is needed, how to put it on, take it off, adjust, and wear it, its limits, and its care. They must show they understand before doing work that needs it.

story_seed: A worker on a new cleaning task kept using the same cloth gloves they wore for boxing parts. A lead asked what the cleaner was, checked the label, and got them chemical-resistant gloves.
crew_questions: Which jobs here have gear that people question or skip, and why?
Has anything changed in your job lately that might need different gear?

title: Eye protection
hazard: Flying chips, dust, chemicals, and bright light can cut, burn, or blind an eye in an instant.
key_points: If a chemical splashes in your eye, get to the eyewash, hold your eyes open, call for help, and keep flushing until help says stop.
Wear safety glasses with side protection whenever something could fly toward your eyes.
Wear goggles for chemical splash, and add a face shield over your glasses or goggles when the task or your site calls for it.
Keep your eye protection on the whole time you are in the hazard area.
Replace eye protection that is scratched, cracked, or loose.
Know where the nearest eyewash is before you start work.
must_say: If something splashes in your eyes, get to the eyewash, keep flushing, and call for help.
never_say: Regular prescription glasses count as safety glasses.
You only need eye protection while your own machine is running.
Rub your eye to get the dust out.

facts.text: Employers must make sure workers use proper eye or face protection when exposed to flying particles, molten metal, liquid chemicals, acids or caustic liquids, chemical gases or vapors, or harmful light.
Eye protection must have side protection when there is a hazard from flying objects.
Workers who wear prescription glasses must wear eye protection with the prescription built in, or protection that fits over their glasses without moving them out of place.

story_seed: A worker walking past a grinding station felt something hit the side of their safety glasses. They found a small metal chip stuck in the side shield.
crew_questions: Where in our area can things fly, splash, or flash toward your eyes?
Where is the nearest eyewash to where you work, and have you used it?

title: Face shields and splash protection
hazard: Splashes of chemicals, hot liquids, or flying debris can burn or cut the face and eyes, and a face shield alone does not fully protect the eyes.
key_points: If a chemical splashes your face or eyes, go to the eyewash or shower now, call for help, and keep flushing until help says stop.
Wear a face shield only over safety glasses or goggles, and wear goggles under it for chemical splash.
Use the face and eye protection listed for the chemical or task by the safety data sheet and your site's rules.
Put the face shield down before you start pouring, spraying, grinding, or pressure cleaning.
Replace face shields that are cracked, scratched, or loose on the headgear.
Keep your shield down until the task is done and the area is safe.
must_say: A face shield goes over safety glasses or goggles, never alone.
never_say: A face shield by itself protects your eyes.
Safety glasses alone are enough for chemical splashes.
You can lift your shield for a better look while you work.

facts.text: Employers must make sure workers use proper eye or face protection when exposed to liquid chemicals, acids or caustic liquids, chemical gases or vapors, flying particles, or molten metal.
Eye and face protection must be clearly marked to show who made it.

story_seed: A worker was transferring cleaner from a drum when the pump hose slipped and sprayed their face shield. The goggles under the shield kept the splash out of their eyes, and they went straight to the eyewash to rinse off.
crew_questions: Which tasks here need a face shield, and is one always there when needed?
What makes people lift or skip their face shield on a task?

title: Wearing hearing protection right
hazard: Loud noise damages hearing for good, and earplugs or earmuffs that are worn wrong or taken out give little protection.
key_points: Wear hearing protection the whole time you are in a noisy area, not just some of the time.
Roll foam earplugs thin, pull your ear up and back, put the plug in, and hold it until it expands.
Make sure earmuffs seal around your ears; hair, hats, and glasses arms can break the seal.
Put earplugs in with clean hands and replace them when dirty or damaged.
Ask for a different size or type if your hearing protection hurts or won't stay in.
Tell your supervisor if your ears ring or sound muffled after work.
must_say: Wear hearing protection the entire time you are in a noisy area.
never_say: Earplugs pushed only partway in still protect you.
You get used to noise, so it stops hurting your hearing.
Earbuds playing music count as hearing protection.

facts.text: Employers must make hearing protectors available at no cost to workers exposed to an 8-hour average of 85 decibels or more, and let them choose from a variety of suitable types.
Employers must train workers in the use and care of hearing protectors, make sure they are fitted correctly at first, and supervise their correct use.
Workers in the hearing conservation program must get training every year on how noise affects hearing, how to choose and wear hearing protectors, and what hearing tests are for.

story_seed: A worker on the packaging line wore their earplugs hanging loose around their neck during a quick fix next to a running machine. A coworker pointed it out, and they put the plugs in properly before going back.
crew_questions: Which hearing protection works best for you here, and why?
When do people pull their hearing protection out in loud areas?

title: How loud is too loud
hazard: Loud noise over time causes permanent hearing loss and ringing in the ears, and it can hide warnings like horns and alarms.
key_points: Treat an area as too loud if you must raise your voice to talk to someone an arm's length away.
Wear hearing protection in all posted noise areas and around loud tools, even for short jobs.
Report new or louder noise, like a loud machine, air leak, or worn bearing.
Go to your hearing tests and ask what your results mean.
Tell your supervisor about ringing ears or muffled hearing after a shift.
Keep guards, covers, and mufflers on equipment because they help keep noise down.
must_say: If you have to raise your voice to be heard at arm's length, wear hearing protection.
never_say: Hearing loss from noise heals overnight.
If it doesn't hurt, it's not too loud.
Short bursts of loud noise don't count.

facts.text: The louder the noise, the shorter the time a worker may be exposed. When noise is over the limits, the employer must use feasible engineering or work-practice controls, and hearing protection when those are not enough.
A hearing conservation program is required when worker noise exposure reaches an 8-hour average of 85 decibels.
Hearing tests must be made available at no cost to workers exposed at or above an 8-hour average of 85 decibels.

story_seed: A worker noticed they had to shout to talk to a coworker standing right next to a new blower. They reported it, and the area was checked and posted as a hearing protection area.
crew_questions: Where in our area do you have to raise your voice to be heard?
Has anyone noticed noise getting louder from a machine or air line lately?
