title: Respirator fit and seal
hazard: A respirator that does not fit or seal lets dust, fumes, or vapors leak in, so the worker breathes in the very hazard it is meant to stop.
key_points: If you smell or taste the contaminant, breathing gets hard, or the seal leaks, leave the area right away and tell your supervisor.
Wear only the make, model, style, and size of respirator you were fit tested on.
Do a seal check every time you put the respirator on.
Be clean-shaven where the respirator seals to your face.
Tell your supervisor about weight changes, dental work, or face changes that could affect fit.
Inspect your respirator before each use and change filters or cartridges as your site's program says.
must_say: Do a seal check every time you put it on. If it leaks, leave the area.
never_say: One size of respirator fits everyone.
A little stubble doesn't affect the seal.
If you can't smell anything, the cartridge is still good.

facts.text: Workers using a tight-fitting respirator must be fit tested before first use, whenever a different size, style, model, or make is used, and at least once a year after that.
Tight-fitting respirators may not be worn by workers with facial hair that comes between the sealing surface and the face, or that gets in the way of the valves.
Workers must do a user seal check every time they put on a tight-fitting respirator, and must leave the work area if they notice vapor or gas getting through, harder breathing, or facepiece leaks.

story_seed: A worker borrowed a coworker's respirator because theirs was in the locker, but it was a different size. During the seal check they felt air leaking at the chin, so they stopped and got their own.
crew_questions: Which jobs here need a respirator, and when were you last fit tested?
What makes it hard to get a good seal here, like heat, other gear, or facial hair rules?

title: Voluntary dust masks
hazard: A dust mask worn for the wrong hazard, or kept dirty, can give false comfort while harmful gases, vapors, or fumes still get into your lungs.
key_points: Read and follow the maker's instructions and warnings before you wear a dust mask.
Check the mask or its box for NIOSH certification and what it is made to protect against.
Never count on a dust mask to stop gases, vapors, fumes, or smoke.
Keep your own mask clean and stored so you never pick up someone else's by mistake.
Tell your supervisor if you think a task needs a required respirator, not just a voluntary dust mask.
must_say: A dust mask filters dust. It does not protect you from gases, vapors, or fumes.
never_say: A dust mask protects you from chemical vapors or welding fumes.
Any mask works as long as it covers your nose and mouth.
Wearing a voluntary dust mask means you can work in an area that requires a respirator.

facts.text: If your employer lets you wear a respirator when one is not required, they must give you the information in OSHA's Appendix D for voluntary users.

OSHA's voluntary-use information tells workers not to wear a respirator into air with contaminants it is not designed to protect against. A dust filter will not protect against gases, vapors, or very small particles of fumes or smoke.
Workers who only wear filtering facepieces (dust masks) voluntarily do not have to be included in a written respiratory protection program.

story_seed: A worker grabbed a dust mask from the shelf before mixing a strong-smelling cleaner, thinking any mask would help. A coworker pointed out the box said it was for dust only, and they stopped to ask the supervisor what the job really needed.
crew_questions: Where on our site do people wear dust masks by choice, and what are they trying to keep out?
Which of our tasks have fumes or vapors that a dust mask would not stop?

title: The right glove for the job
hazard: The wrong glove lets chemicals soak through, lets blades cut through, or lets heat burn your hands, and any glove can get caught and pull your hand into rotating parts.
key_points: Take off gloves and rings, secure loose sleeves, and tie back long hair before working near drills, lathes, or other rotating parts.
Match the glove to the hazard: cut, chemical, heat, or puncture, as your site's glove chart or supervisor says.
Check the chemical label or safety data sheet to find which glove material resists that chemical.
Inspect gloves before each use and replace any with holes, tears, swelling, or stiffness.
Ask for a different size or type if your gloves do not fit or slow you down.
must_say: Never wear gloves near rotating parts. Take them off, do not look for a better glove.
never_say: Any glove is better than no glove.
A tighter or thicker glove makes it safe to work near rotating parts.
One type of glove works for every chemical.

facts.text: Employers must select and require hand protection when hands face hazards like skin absorption of harmful substances, severe cuts, punctures, chemical burns, thermal burns, and harmful temperature extremes.
Glove selection must be based on how the glove performs for the task, the conditions, how long it is used, and the hazards found.

story_seed: A worker reached for a cut-resistant glove before pouring a cleaning chemical, then noticed the label called for a chemical-resistant glove instead. They swapped gloves before starting.
crew_questions: Which jobs on our site need a different glove than the one most of us grab?
Where on our site are there rotating parts where gloves must come off?

title: Foot protection
hazard: Falling or rolling objects can crush toes, sharp objects can pierce the sole, and some areas carry static or shock hazards that the right footwear helps control.
key_points: Wear the protective footwear your site requires in every area where it is required.
Inspect your boots for cracked soles, exposed toe caps, deep cuts, or worn tread, and replace damaged pairs.
Ask which footwear rating you need if you work near electrical or static hazards.
Keep your feet out from under loads, pallet jacks, and rolling carts.
Never cut or modify safety footwear.
must_say: Wear your protective footwear every time you are in an area that requires it.
never_say: Regular sneakers are fine if you are careful.
Safety toes make it okay to put your feet under a load.
Any boot labeled for work meets every hazard rating.

facts.text: Employers must make sure workers use protective footwear where there is a danger of foot injury from falling or rolling objects or objects piercing the sole.
Protective footwear is also required when it will protect a worker from an electrical hazard, such as static discharge or electric shock, that remains after other protective steps are taken.
Protective footwear must meet a listed consensus standard, or be shown to be at least as effective.

story_seed: A worker stepping back from a pallet felt a pallet jack wheel roll onto the front of their boot. The safety toe held, and the crew talked about keeping feet clear of moving equipment.
crew_questions: Where on our site are falling, rolling, or sharp objects most likely to reach our feet?
How do we get worn-out safety footwear replaced here?

title: Hard hats and bump caps
hazard: Falling objects and contact with exposed electrical parts can cause serious head injuries, and a bump cap is not built to stop them.
key_points: Wear a hard hat wherever objects could fall on your head, as your site requires.
Use only a bump cap where your site allows it, and never in place of a hard hat.
Wear an electrical-rated hard hat when working near exposed electrical parts that could touch your head.
Inspect the shell and suspension before each shift and replace any hard hat that is cracked, dented, or has been struck.
Follow the maker's instructions for cleaning, storage, and what can be stuck on the shell.
must_say: A bump cap is not a hard hat. Wear a hard hat wherever things can fall.
never_say: A bump cap protects you from falling objects.
Any hard hat is fine near live electrical parts.
A hard hat that took a hit is fine if you cannot see a crack.

facts.text: Employers must make sure workers wear a protective helmet where there is a potential for head injury from falling objects.
Workers near exposed electrical conductors that could contact the head must wear a helmet designed to reduce electrical shock hazard.
Head protection must meet one of the listed ANSI consensus standards, or be shown to be at least as effective.

story_seed: A worker wearing a bump cap walked under a mezzanine where a crew was moving parts overhead. A coworker stopped them and handed them a hard hat before they went through.
crew_questions: Where on our site is a bump cap okay, and where is a hard hat required?
When did you last check your hard hat's suspension, and what would make you replace it?

title: Read the label
hazard: Using a chemical without reading its label can lead to burns, poisoning, breathing harm, or fire.
key_points: Read the label before you open, pour, or use any chemical.
Look for the signal word, the pictograms, and the hazard statements first.
Follow the precautionary statements for protective gear, handling, and first aid.
Never remove or cover a label on an incoming container.
Stop and ask your supervisor if a label is missing, damaged, or hard to read.
must_say: If there is no label, do not use it. Tell your supervisor.
never_say: If you have used a chemical before, you do not need to read the label.
A 'Warning' label means the chemical is safe.
You can tell what is in a container by its color or smell.

facts.text: Labels on shipped chemical containers must show a product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, and the maker's or supplier's name, address, and phone number.
The signal words are 'Danger' for more severe hazards and 'Warning' for less severe hazards.
Employers must not remove or deface labels on incoming chemical containers unless the container is right away marked with the required information.

story_seed: A worker was about to use a new degreaser the same way as the old one. They read the label first and saw it needed a different glove and more ventilation.
crew_questions: Which chemicals in our area have the signal word 'Danger' on them?
What do we do here when we find a container with a missing or worn label?

title: Safety data sheets
hazard: Not knowing a chemical's hazards, first aid, and spill steps can turn a small exposure or spill into a serious injury.
key_points: Help an exposed person first: flush at the eyewash or get them to fresh air, call for help, then check the safety data sheet.
Know where to find safety data sheets for your area, on paper or electronic, before you need them.
Look up the protective gear section before working with a new chemical.
Read the accidental release section before cleaning up any spill.
Ask your supervisor if you cannot find or understand a safety data sheet.
must_say: Know where your safety data sheets are before an emergency happens.
never_say: Safety data sheets are only for managers or safety staff.
If the safety data sheet is hard to find, guess based on a similar chemical.
You only need the label, never the safety data sheet.

facts.text: Employers must have a safety data sheet (SDS) in the workplace for each hazardous chemical they use.
Safety data sheets must be readily accessible to workers in their work area during each work shift. Electronic access is allowed if it creates no barriers to immediate access.

An SDS has 16 sections in a set order, including First-aid measures (Section 4), Fire-fighting measures (Section 5), Accidental release measures (Section 6), and Exposure controls/personal protection (Section 8).

story_seed: A worker got a splash of cleaner on their arm and flushed it at the eyewash right away, but no one on the crew knew where the safety data sheets were kept. After that, the crew walked to the safety data sheet station together and practiced finding the first-aid section.
crew_questions: Where are the safety data sheets for our area, and how do we reach them on night shift?
If someone got splashed, what would you do first, and who would pull up the safety data sheet?

title: Labeling bottles and secondary containers
hazard: An unlabeled bottle or bucket can be mistaken for water or a different chemical, leading to burns, poisoning, or dangerous mixing.
key_points: Label any container you pour a chemical into before someone else could use or move it.
Use your site's workplace labels with the product name and its hazards.
Never put chemicals in food or drink containers.
Never use a chemical from an unlabeled container; tell your supervisor.
Replace labels that are worn, faded, or hard to read.
must_say: If you pour it into another container, label it, unless you alone will use it all right away.
never_say: Everyone knows what is in the blue spray bottle, so it does not need a label.
It is fine to reuse a drink bottle for a chemical if you write on it later.
Leftover chemicals can go back in any empty container.

facts.text: Each container of hazardous chemicals in the workplace must be labeled with the product identifier and words, pictures, or symbols that give general information about its hazards, or with the full shipped-container label information.
A portable container does not need a label only if the chemical came from a labeled container and is for the immediate use of the person who did the transfer.
Workplace labels must be legible, in English, and prominently displayed. Other languages may be added as long as English is also shown.

story_seed: At shift change, a worker found an unlabeled spray bottle on a cart and almost used it on a food-contact surface. They set it aside and asked the previous shift what was in it.
crew_questions: Which bottles or buckets in our area get filled from bigger containers, and are they labeled?
Where do we get blank workplace labels here?

title: Flammable liquid storage
hazard: Flammable liquids give off vapors that can catch fire or explode from a spark, flame, or hot surface.
key_points: Keep flammable liquids in closed, approved containers and safety cans when not in use.
Return flammable liquids to the flammable storage cabinet or room when you are done.
Never smoke or use open flames in flammable liquid storage areas.
Keep cabinet doors closed and never block or prop them open.
Follow your site's procedure for bonding and grounding when you transfer flammable liquids.
must_say: No smoking and no open flames where flammable liquids are stored.
never_say: Flammable liquids only burn if you pour them on a fire.
It is fine to leave a flammable cabinet door propped open for convenience.
Any container with a lid is good enough for gasoline or solvent.

facts.text: Open flames and smoking are not permitted in flammable liquid storage areas.
A safety can is an approved container of not more than 5 gallons, with a spring-closing lid and spout cover, designed to relieve internal pressure in a fire.
Flammable storage cabinets must be labeled 'Flammable—Keep Fire Away' in conspicuous lettering.

story_seed: A worker found an open can of solvent left on a bench near a grinder at the end of shift. They closed it and put it back in the flammable cabinet before anyone started grinding.
crew_questions: Where do flammable liquids end up outside the cabinet in our area during a shift?
What ignition sources are near where we use or store flammable liquids?

title: Compressed gas cylinders
hazard: A damaged or knocked-over cylinder can release gas under high pressure, turn into a missile, feed a fire, or leak a toxic or flammable gas.
key_points: Secure cylinders upright so they cannot be knocked over, as your site's procedure requires.
Keep the valve cap on, hand-tight, whenever the cylinder is not in use or connected for use.
Close cylinder valves when work is finished and on empty cylinders.
Never drop cylinders, lift them by the cap, or use them as rollers or supports.
Keep oxygen cylinders and fittings free of oil and grease, and never handle them with oily hands or gloves.
must_say: Before moving a cylinder, remove the regulator and cap the valve, unless it is secured on a cylinder cart.
never_say: An empty cylinder is harmless, so it does not need its valve closed.
A little oil on an oxygen fitting helps it seal.
You can lift a cylinder by its valve cap.

facts.text: Valve protection caps must be in place, hand-tight, except when the cylinder is in use or connected for use.

Stored oxygen cylinders must be kept at least 20 feet from fuel-gas cylinders or combustible materials, or separated by a noncombustible barrier at least 5 feet high with a fire-resistance rating of at least one-half hour.
Unless cylinders are secured on a special cart made for them, regulators must be removed and valve caps put in place before cylinders are moved.

story_seed: A worker saw a stored oxygen cylinder standing loose with no chain and no cap, right beside the fuel-gas cylinders. They chained and capped it and told the lead it needed to be moved away from the fuel gas.
crew_questions: Where on our site are cylinders stored or used, and are they always secured?
How do we move cylinders here, and what equipment do we use?

title: Hot work and welding fire safety
hazard: Sparks, slag, and heat from welding, cutting, or grinding can travel far and start fires that smolder long after the work stops.
key_points: Get the hot work permit or authorization your site requires before you start.
Move combustibles away from the work, or cover and shield what cannot be moved.
Keep a charged fire extinguisher ready at the work area.
Post a fire watch when your site's permit calls for one, and keep watching after the work ends.
Stop hot work right away if conditions change or the area cannot be made safe.
must_say: If the area cannot be made safe, do not do the hot work.
never_say: Once the welding stops, the fire risk is over.
It is fine to weld in a sprinklered building while the sprinklers are shut off.
Sparks only fall straight down, so a few feet of clearance is enough.

facts.text: Before cutting or welding, the area must be inspected by the person responsible for authorizing it, who sets the precautions, preferably in a written permit.
Where practicable, combustibles must be moved at least 35 feet from the work site, or protected with flameproofed covers or shields.
When a fire watch is required, it must be kept for at least a half hour after welding or cutting ends to catch smoldering fires.

story_seed: After a cutting job ended, the fire watch stayed and noticed smoke rising from cardboard behind a wall opening. They put it out with the extinguisher they had kept ready.
crew_questions: Where on our site do sparks have a path to reach combustibles, like floor gaps or wall openings?
Who authorizes hot work here, and how do we get a permit?

title: Small chemical spills
hazard: Spilled chemicals can burn skin, give off harmful vapors, catch fire, or react with other materials, and slips on spills cause falls.
key_points: Get away and warn others if the spill is large, unknown, fuming, or anyone is hurt, then call for help per your site's plan.
Clean up only small spills you are trained for and that your site's procedure allows.
Check the label or safety data sheet before cleanup to know the hazards and protective gear.
Use your site's spill kit and protective gear, and keep others away from the area.
Report every spill to your supervisor, even small ones you cleaned up.
must_say: If you do not know what it is, or it is too big, get away and call for help.
never_say: Mix another chemical in to neutralize any spill.
Just wipe it with whatever rags are around.
Small spills do not need to be reported.

facts.text: Every safety data sheet must include an 'Accidental release measures' section.
Chemical safety training must cover how workers can protect themselves, including work practices, emergency procedures, and protective equipment the employer has set up.

story_seed: A worker noticed a puddle under a drum and was about to wipe it up with a shop towel. They checked the label first, saw it was corrosive, and got the spill kit and gloves the safety data sheet called for.
crew_questions: Where is the nearest spill kit to our area, and what is in it?
Which spills in our area are too big or too hazardous for us to clean up ourselves?

title: Eyewash and drench showers
hazard: Corrosive chemicals in the eyes or on the skin can cause lasting damage within moments if they are not flushed off right away.
key_points: Get to the eyewash or shower right away if a corrosive chemical splashes in your eyes or on your body.
Hold your eyelids open and keep flushing until medical help or your site's procedure says to stop. Do not stop early.
Remove contaminated clothing while under the shower, and get medical help.
Know where the nearest eyewash and shower are, and keep the path to them clear.
Report any eyewash or shower that is blocked, dirty, or not working.
must_say: If it splashes in your eyes, get to the eyewash now and keep flushing. Have someone call for medical help.
never_say: Rub your eyes to get the chemical out.
A quick splash of water is enough.
Finish your task first, then go to the eyewash.

facts.text: Where the eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, facilities for quick drenching or flushing of the eyes and body must be provided within the work area for immediate emergency use.

story_seed: A worker found a pallet parked in front of the eyewash station during a busy shift. They moved it and reminded the crew that someone with chemical in their eyes cannot get around obstacles.
crew_questions: Can you walk to the nearest eyewash from your spot with your eyes closed, and is the path clear?
Who checks our eyewash stations, and what do we do if one is not working?

title: Acids and caustics
hazard: Acids and caustics can burn skin and eyes, damage lungs, and react violently when mixed with the wrong chemicals.
key_points: Flush right away at the eyewash or shower if you are splashed, keep flushing, and have someone call for medical help.
Wear the eye, face, hand, and body protection the safety data sheet and your site require.
Never mix acids and caustics or other chemicals unless your site's procedure says to.
Keep containers closed, labeled, and stored apart as your site requires.
Know where the nearest eyewash and shower are before you start.
must_say: If you are splashed, flush with water right away and keep flushing. Have someone call for medical help.
never_say: Put a base on an acid burn to neutralize it.
Caustics are less dangerous than acids.
Safety glasses alone are enough when pouring corrosives.

facts.text: Where the eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, facilities for quick drenching or flushing must be provided within the work area for immediate emergency use.
Every safety data sheet must include sections on first-aid measures and on exposure controls and personal protection.

story_seed: A worker was about to top off a caustic cleaning tank wearing only safety glasses. A coworker reminded them the safety data sheet called for goggles and a face shield, and they went back to get them.
crew_questions: Which acids or caustics do we use in our area, and what protective gear does each one need?
Where could an acid and a caustic get mixed by mistake on our site?

title: Carbon monoxide from engines
hazard: Engines on forklifts, trucks, and other equipment give off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can cause headaches, confusion, collapse, and death.
key_points: Shut off engines and get anyone with headache, dizziness, or confusion to fresh air; call 911 if anyone is confused, very sick, or passes out.
Never idle engines in closed areas, trailers, or near air intakes.
Keep doors and ventilation open as your site requires when engine-powered equipment runs indoors.
Report forklifts or equipment that run rough or smell of strong exhaust for maintenance.
Tell your supervisor if you or others feel sick when engines are running nearby.
Never go into a closed trailer or room where someone collapsed near a running engine; call 911.
must_say: If someone gets dizzy or confused near running engines, get them to fresh air and call 911.
never_say: You will smell carbon monoxide before it hurts you.
Propane forklifts do not make carbon monoxide.
Opening one door makes it safe to idle a truck inside all day.

facts.text: Carbon monoxide from powered industrial truck operations must not exceed the limits set in OSHA's air contaminant rules.
OSHA's exposure limit for carbon monoxide is 50 parts per million (ppm), averaged over an 8-hour work shift.
Forklift operator training must cover closed areas where poor ventilation or poor maintenance could cause a buildup of carbon monoxide or diesel exhaust.

story_seed: On a cold day with the dock doors shut, several workers near a propane forklift started getting headaches. One spoke up, the truck was shut off, everyone went outside to fresh air and got checked, and the truck was sent for maintenance.
crew_questions: Where on our site do engines run indoors, especially when doors are closed in cold weather?
What would you do if a coworker near a running engine seemed confused or sick?

title: Silica dust
hazard: Breathing fine crystalline silica dust from cutting, grinding, or crushing stone, concrete, sand, or brick can scar the lungs and cause lung disease and cancer.
key_points: Use the water, dust collection, or ventilation your site provides every time you cut, grind, or crush silica materials.
Never dry sweep or use compressed air to clean silica dust; use wet methods or a HEPA vacuum.
Wear the respirator your site requires for the task, and keep it clean and fitted.
Keep out of marked regulated areas unless you are authorized.
Report dust controls that are broken, clogged, or not working.
must_say: Never dry sweep or blow silica dust with compressed air.
never_say: If you cannot see the dust, it cannot hurt you.
A cloth over your face is enough for silica dust.
Blowing dust off with compressed air is the fastest safe way to clean up.

facts.text: OSHA's limit for respirable crystalline silica is 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, averaged over an 8-hour day.
Dry sweeping or dry brushing is not allowed where it could add to silica exposure, unless wet sweeping, HEPA vacuuming, or other low-exposure methods are not feasible.
Employers must offer medical exams at no cost to workers exposed at or above the action level of 25 micrograms per cubic meter of air (8-hour average) for 30 or more days per year.

story_seed: At the end of a shift, a worker reached for an air hose to blow concrete dust off a bench. A coworker handed them the HEPA vacuum instead.
crew_questions: Which tasks or materials on our site make silica dust?
How do we clean up dust in our area now, and is there a safer way?

title: Bloodborne pathogens
hazard: Contact with someone else's blood or certain body fluids, through cuts, needle sticks, or splashes to eyes or mouth, can spread infections like hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.
key_points: Call 911 and your site's first aid responders when someone is badly hurt, and put on gloves before touching blood.
Wash your hands and skin with soap and water right away after any contact with blood.
Never pick up broken glass that may have blood on it with your hands; use a brush and dust pan or tongs.
Leave blood cleanup to people trained and assigned by your site.
Report any blood contact or needle stick to your supervisor right away.
must_say: Report any contact with someone else's blood right away.
never_say: If the person looks healthy, their blood is safe to touch.
Bare hands are fine for a small cut on a coworker.
You only need to report a needle stick if you feel sick later.

facts.text: Employees must wash hands and other skin with soap and water, or flush eyes, nose, or mouth with water, immediately or as soon as feasible after contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials.
Broken glassware that may be contaminated must not be picked up directly with the hands. Use a brush and dust pan, tongs, or forceps.

story_seed: A worker cut their hand on a box cutter and a coworker reached to help with bare hands. Another coworker handed over gloves from the first aid kit first.
crew_questions: Who on our site is trained to clean up blood, and how do we reach them?
Where are the gloves in our first aid kits, and are they stocked?

title: Compressed air is not a broom
hazard: Compressed air can drive chips and dust into eyes and skin, and air forced into the body through skin or openings can cause serious injury.
key_points: Use a brush, vacuum, or other method your site approves instead of compressed air when you can.
Never point compressed air at yourself or anyone else, or use it to clean clothes or skin.
Use only air nozzles your site approves for cleaning, with chip guarding.
Wear eye protection and other protective gear when using compressed air.
Check that no one is in the path of flying chips before you start.
must_say: Never blow compressed air at yourself or anyone else.
never_say: Blowing off your clothes with shop air is a quick way to get clean.
Low-pressure air is safe to point at people.
Compressed air horseplay is harmless.

facts.text: Compressed air must not be used for cleaning unless it is reduced to less than 30 psi, and then only with effective chip guarding and protective equipment.
Employers are responsible for the safe condition of tools and equipment workers use, including tools workers bring themselves.

story_seed: At the end of a shift, a worker started to blow metal chips off their pants with an air hose. A coworker stopped them, and they used a brush instead.
crew_questions: Where on our site do people reach for an air hose to clean, and what could we use instead?
Are the air nozzles in our area the approved type?

title: Your emergency action plan
hazard: In a fire, chemical release, or other emergency, people who do not know the alarms, routes, and meeting points can be trapped or hurt.
key_points: Know how to report a fire or emergency at your site.
Learn what each alarm sound means and what you must do when you hear it.
Know your exit routes and your assembly point.
Know who to ask about the plan and your duties in it.
Ask for a review of the plan when your job or the plan changes.
must_say: When the alarm sounds, follow the plan. Get out by your route and go to your meeting point.
never_say: Finish your task before responding to the alarm.
The emergency plan is only for managers.
Every alarm means the same thing.

facts.text: An emergency action plan must include how to report emergencies, how to evacuate and which exit routes to use, how to account for all employees after evacuating, and duties for anyone doing rescue or medical work.
Employers must use an employee alarm system with a distinctive signal for each purpose.
Employers must review the plan with each covered employee when the plan is developed or the employee is first assigned, when their duties under it change, and when the plan changes.

story_seed: During a drill, a new worker heard an alarm tone they had never heard before and did not know if it meant evacuate or shelter. Their lead walked them through what each signal meant afterward.
crew_questions: What alarm sounds do we have on our site, and what does each one mean?
Who is the contact for our emergency plan, and when was it last reviewed with you?

title: Exit routes and doors
hazard: Blocked, locked, or hidden exits can trap people during a fire or other emergency.
key_points: Keep exit routes, aisles, and exit doors clear of materials and equipment at all times.
Never lock, chain, or block an exit door.
Report exit signs that are dark, damaged, or hidden.
Know every way out of your work area, not just the door you usually use.
Report any exit door that is hard to open or will not open.
must_say: Never block or lock an exit, even for a minute.
never_say: It is fine to stack pallets in front of an exit if you move them later.
Exit doors can be locked to keep people from leaving early.
Everyone knows where the exits are, so signs are not needed.

facts.text: Employees must be able to open an exit route door from the inside at all times without keys, tools, or special knowledge.
An exit access must be at least 28 inches wide at all points.
Exit routes must be free and unobstructed, and no materials or equipment may be placed in them, even temporarily.

story_seed: A worker found a stack of empty totes blocking the side exit during a busy receiving day. They cleared it and told the lead so it would not happen again.
crew_questions: Which exit in our area most often gets blocked, and why?
If your usual exit was full of smoke, which way would you go?

title: Fire extinguishers
hazard: Fires grow fast, and trying to fight a fire that is too big, or without training, can trap or burn you.
key_points: Sound the alarm and call for help first, before anything else.
Follow your site's plan: if it says evacuate only, get out and do not fight the fire.
Use an extinguisher only if you are trained and allowed, the fire is small, and you have a clear way out.
Keep extinguishers visible, mounted, and free of blocking materials.
Report extinguishers that are missing, used, damaged, or low on pressure.
must_say: Sound the alarm first. If the fire is not small or you are not trained, get out.
never_say: Everyone should try to put out a fire before leaving.
Any extinguisher works on any fire.
Fight the fire even if the plan says evacuate.

facts.text: Where extinguishers are provided for employee use, employers must train employees on their use and the hazards of fighting early-stage fires when first hired and at least annually after that.
Portable extinguishers must be visually inspected monthly and get an annual maintenance check.
For Class A fires, extinguishers must be placed so employees travel 75 feet or less to reach one.

story_seed: A small fire started in a trash bin near a work cell. The worker pulled the alarm first, then, because they were trained and their site allows it, used the nearby extinguisher with their back to the exit, and the fire went out.
crew_questions: Does our site plan say to fight small fires or to evacuate only, and who is allowed to use extinguishers?
Where is the nearest extinguisher to where you work right now?

title: Fire prevention
hazard: Piles of combustible waste, poor chemical storage, and uncontrolled heat or sparks can start fires that spread quickly.
key_points: Clear away combustible waste like cardboard and dust, and put oily rags in the closed container your site provides.
Store flammable and hazardous materials only where your site says.
Keep heat sources, sparks, and open flames away from combustibles.
Report damaged cords, overheating equipment, and broken safeguards on heaters or ovens.
Know the fire hazards in your area and who controls them.
must_say: Keep your area clean. Combustible waste is fuel for a fire.
never_say: A little dust or cardboard pile is no fire risk.
Oily rags can go in any trash can.
Fire prevention is only the maintenance team's job.

facts.text: A fire prevention plan must list major fire hazards, how to handle and store hazardous materials, potential ignition sources and their control, and the fire protection equipment needed.
The plan must include procedures to control buildup of flammable and combustible waste.
Employers must tell employees about the fire hazards they are exposed to when first assigned to a job.

story_seed: A worker noticed a pile of oily rags stuffed behind a warm machine at the end of shift. They moved them to the proper waste container and reported it.
crew_questions: Where does combustible waste pile up in our area during a shift?
What heat sources or spark sources are close to combustibles here?

title: Evacuation and headcount
hazard: If people are not counted after an evacuation, someone missing may go unnoticed, or others may go back in and get hurt.
key_points: Leave right away by your assigned route when the evacuation alarm sounds.
Go straight to your assembly point and check in for the headcount.
Never go back inside until the people in charge say it is safe.
Tell the person taking the headcount if you know someone is missing or where they were.
Follow the directions of your site's trained evacuation helpers.
must_say: Never go back inside for anyone or anything. Tell responders who is missing.
never_say: Go back in and look for missing coworkers yourself.
You can skip the assembly point if you leave the site.
Stop to grab your belongings before evacuating.

facts.text: An emergency action plan must include procedures to account for all employees after evacuation.
Employers must designate and train employees to help with a safe and orderly evacuation of other employees.

story_seed: During a drill, a worker left by the back door and went to their car instead of the assembly point. The headcount showed them missing, and the crew talked about what that would mean for responders in a real fire.
crew_questions: Where is our assembly point, and who takes the headcount for our area?
How would visitors or contractors in our area be counted?

title: Severe weather and sheltering
hazard: Tornadoes, lightning, and severe storms can cause flying debris, building damage, and electrical strikes that injure people caught in the open or in the wrong spot.
key_points: Go to your site's designated shelter area right away when a severe weather alert or alarm sounds.
Move indoors when you hear thunder or see lightning, as your site's procedure says.
Stay in the shelter area until the people in charge give the all-clear.
Know how your site warns you about severe weather and where to go from your area.
Check in for the headcount after sheltering.
must_say: When the severe weather alarm sounds, go to your shelter area now.
never_say: Stay by the windows to watch the storm.
Shelter in a trailer or vehicle during a tornado.
Keep working outside until the rain starts.

facts.text: An emergency action plan must include procedures for emergency evacuation, including the type of evacuation and exit route assignments.
Employers must have and maintain an employee alarm system with a distinctive signal for each purpose.

story_seed: A storm warning came over the radio while a crew was loading trailers at the dock. One worker knew the shelter signal and led the crew to the designated room before the wind picked up.
crew_questions: Where is the severe weather shelter area closest to where you work?
How do we get warned about severe weather on our site, especially outside or at the dock?

title: First aid on site
hazard: Delays in getting help after an injury can make it much worse, and untrained or unprotected helpers can be hurt themselves.
key_points: Call 911 right away for serious injuries, then call your site's first aid responders.
Check the area is safe first; never touch someone in contact with electricity or enter a confined space after them. Call 911.
Know who the trained first aid responders are on your shift and how to reach them.
Know where first aid kits are, and report kits that are empty or missing supplies.
Put on gloves before touching blood or body fluids.
must_say: For a serious injury, call 911 first. Do not wait.
never_say: Move a badly injured person right away even if they might have a neck or back injury.
Only call 911 after a supervisor says it is okay.
Gloves are optional when helping with a bleeding injury.

facts.text: If there is no infirmary, clinic, or hospital near the workplace, a person or persons must be adequately trained to give first aid.
Adequate first aid supplies must be readily available.
If workers may be exposed to blood while using first aid supplies, employers must provide protective equipment such as gloves.

story_seed: A worker got a deep cut on night shift, and the crew could not find the first aid kit or remember who was trained. After that, the lead posted the responder names and kit locations at the break room.
crew_questions: Who are the trained first aid responders on our shift, and how do we reach them?
Where is the nearest first aid kit, and when did someone last check it?

title: Reporting serious injuries to OSHA
hazard: When serious injuries are not reported quickly inside the company, the site can miss required reports to OSHA and the hazard may hurt someone else.
key_points: Call 911 first for any serious injury, then tell your supervisor right away.
Tell your supervisor right away if a coworker is admitted to a hospital, loses an eye, or has an amputation from a work incident.
Report serious injuries even if they happen at the end of a shift or off-hours.
Leave the scene as it is unless changing it is needed to help someone or prevent more harm.
Follow your site's procedure for who makes the report to OSHA.
must_say: Tell your supervisor about any serious injury right away, so the site can report it on time.
never_say: Serious injuries only need to be reported at the end of the week.
Hold off reporting until you know if the person will be okay.
Only fatalities ever need to be reported to OSHA.

facts.text: Under federal OSHA rules, employers must report a work-related death to OSHA within eight (8) hours.

Under federal OSHA rules, employers must report a work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye to OSHA within twenty-four (24) hours, if it happens within 24 hours of the incident.

story_seed: A worker was taken to the hospital after a late-shift incident, and the crew assumed someone else had told the supervisor. The next morning they learned no one had, and the crew agreed to always call the supervisor directly.
crew_questions: Who do you call on our site if a serious injury happens on nights or weekends?
What gets in the way of reporting an injury right away here?

title: Report every injury
hazard: Small injuries that go unreported can get worse without care, and the hazard that caused them stays in place to hurt someone else.
key_points: Get first aid or medical care first when you are hurt.
Report every work injury or illness to your supervisor right away, even if it seems minor.
Report close calls and the hazards behind them too.
Follow your site's procedure for how and where to report.
Speak up if you feel pressure not to report an injury.
must_say: Report every work injury or illness to your supervisor right away, even if it seems small.
never_say: Reporting an injury will get you in trouble.
Only report injuries that need a doctor.
Keep minor injuries to yourself so the team's record stays clean.

facts.text: Employers must set up a reasonable way for employees to report work injuries and illnesses promptly and accurately. A procedure that would discourage reporting is not reasonable.
Federal rules say employees have the right to report work-related injuries and illnesses, and employers must not fire or in any way discriminate against employees for reporting.

story_seed: A worker felt a pull in their back lifting a box but decided not to say anything. A week later it was worse, and when they finally reported it, the crew found the shelf height was causing the problem for others too.
crew_questions: How do you report an injury on our site, and is it easy to do?
What might keep someone here from reporting a small injury?

title: Near misses are free lessons
hazard: A near miss that nobody reports is a warning ignored, and the same hazard can hurt someone the next time.
key_points: Stop and make the area safe first if the hazard is still there.
Report every near miss to your supervisor the same shift, even if nobody was hurt.
Tell what happened and what almost happened, not who to blame.
Follow your site's procedure for writing up near misses.
Ask what was changed after a report, so the fix really happens.
must_say: If it almost hurt someone, report it today.
A near miss is a free lesson. Report it so nobody gets hurt next time.
never_say: Near misses don't count because nobody got hurt.
Reporting a near miss will get you or your coworker in trouble.
Only report it if a supervisor saw it.
story_seed: A pallet slid off a forklift's forks and landed where a worker had been standing a moment before. The driver almost kept quiet, but the report led to a fix in how loads were stacked.
crew_questions: What near miss have you seen here that never got reported?
What makes it hard to report a near miss on our site, and how can we make it easier?

title: Heat illness: know the signs
hazard: Working in heat can overheat the body, leading to heat exhaustion and heat stroke, which can kill.
key_points: Call 911 right away if someone is confused, passes out, has a seizure, or stops making sense; that can be heat stroke.
Cool a person with heat stroke right now while waiting for help: move them to shade, remove extra clothing, and wet them down.
Watch for early signs: heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, cramps, nausea, or feeling weak.
Stop work and get to a cool place as soon as you or a coworker feel these signs.
Never leave a person who feels sick from heat alone.
Follow your site's heat plan for water, rest, and shade.
must_say: Confusion or passing out in the heat is an emergency. Call 911 and start cooling them now.
Never leave a sick worker alone in the heat.
never_say: Someone with heat stroke just needs to drink water and rest.
If they stopped sweating, they are cooling down and are fine.
There is a federal OSHA heat standard you must follow.
story_seed: A worker on a hot loading dock started slurring words and stumbling. A coworker called 911 and the crew moved him to shade and soaked him with cool water until help came.
crew_questions: Where on our site does it get hottest, and where is the nearest cool spot?
How would you get help fast if a coworker started acting confused in the heat?

title: New to the heat
hazard: Workers who are new to the heat or back from time off have bodies that are not used to it yet, so they can get heat sick fast.
key_points: Call 911 and start cooling someone right away if they get confused or pass out in the heat.
Build up time in the heat slowly when you are new or coming back from time off.
Take the rest and water breaks your site's heat plan gives you, even if you feel fine.
Watch new coworkers closely and check on them often during hot shifts.
Tell your supervisor if you are new to the heat or have been away from work.
must_say: New and returning workers need time to get used to the heat. Build up slowly and check on each other.
never_say: Tough workers don't need time to get used to heat.
If you worked in the heat last year, you are already used to it.
There is a federal OSHA heat standard that sets the schedule.
story_seed: On his first hot week back after time off, a worker skipped breaks to keep up with the crew and got dizzy. A lead noticed, sat him in the shade, and adjusted his workload.
crew_questions: Who on our crew is new or just back, and how are we looking out for them?
How does our site help people get used to working in the heat?

title: Cold stress
hazard: Cold, wet, and windy conditions can drop body temperature and freeze skin, causing hypothermia and frostbite.
key_points: Call 911 if someone is shivering hard, then stops, or becomes confused or very sleepy; get them to a warm place.
Wear layers, a hat, and gloves that fit the task, and keep a dry set of clothes.
Change out of wet clothes as soon as you can.
Take warm-up breaks in a heated area as your site allows.
Watch coworkers for numb, pale, or waxy skin on fingers, toes, ears, and face.
Never rub frostbitten skin; warm it gently and get medical help.
must_say: Confusion or very slow, sleepy behavior in the cold is an emergency. Call 911 and get them warm.
never_say: Rub frostbitten skin hard to warm it up.
A drink of alcohol will warm you up in the cold.
If they stop shivering, they are getting better.
story_seed: A worker in a freezer area kept going in damp gloves and lost feeling in his fingers. A coworker noticed, sent him to the break room to warm up, and reported it to the supervisor.
crew_questions: Where on our site do people get coldest or wettest?
What do we have here to help people warm up and stay dry?

title: Water, rest, shade
hazard: Without enough water, rest, and shade, workers in heat can quickly get heat exhaustion or heat stroke.
key_points: Call 911 and cool the person now if someone in the heat is confused or passes out; water alone will not fix heat stroke.
Drink water often during the shift, even before you feel thirsty.
Take rest breaks in shade or a cool area when it is hot.
Know where water and cool rest areas are before the shift starts.
Speak up if water runs low or shade is missing.
Follow your site's heat plan for breaks.
must_say: Drink water often and rest in shade. If someone is confused in the heat, call 911 and cool them now.
never_say: Water is the cure for heat stroke.
Skipping breaks shows you are a hard worker.
Only drink water when you feel thirsty.
story_seed: A crew working outside on a hot afternoon found the water cooler empty. One worker spoke up, the lead brought more water and set up a shaded rest spot before work went on.
crew_questions: Where is the closest water and shade from where you work today?
What gets in the way of taking breaks when it is hot here?

title: Fatigue and long shifts
hazard: Tired workers react slower and make more mistakes, which can lead to crashes, falls, and caught-in injuries.
key_points: Tell your supervisor if you are too tired to work safely, especially before driving or running equipment.
Take your breaks and use them to rest.
Watch coworkers for signs of fatigue like nodding off, missed steps, or slow reactions.
Plan for safe sleep before shifts, especially when working nights or overtime.
Never run machines or drive a forklift when you are fighting to stay awake.
must_say: If you are too tired to work safely, tell your supervisor before you start the task.
never_say: Energy drinks fix fatigue.
Pushing through tiredness is part of the job.
You can't get hurt from being tired.
story_seed: Near the end of a double shift, a forklift driver almost backed into a coworker because he zoned out. He parked the truck and told his lead he was too tired to drive safely.
crew_questions: When are people most tired on our shifts, and what tasks are riskiest then?
How can someone here say they are too tired without feeling judged?

title: Repetitive motion and strains
hazard: Doing the same motion over and over, especially with force or awkward positions, can injure muscles, tendons, and nerves.
key_points: Report early signs like pain, tingling, numbness, or swelling to your supervisor right away.
Switch hands or tasks when your site allows, and use job rotation if it is offered.
Keep work close to your body and avoid bending or twisting your wrists.
Use the right tool so you don't have to squeeze or force it.
Take short breaks to stretch and change position.
must_say: Report pain, tingling, or numbness early. Don't wait until it gets worse.
never_say: Pain is normal and will go away if you keep working.
Only lifting heavy things causes strain injuries.
Reporting aches makes you look weak.
story_seed: A packer felt tingling in her hand for weeks and kept quiet. When she finally reported it, her lead found the tape gun was hard to squeeze and replaced it.
crew_questions: Which tasks here make your hands, wrists, or shoulders ache?
What small change would make your most repetitive task easier on your body?

title: Set up your work area
hazard: A poorly set-up work area forces awkward reaches, bending, and twisting that can strain your back, neck, and arms.
key_points: Set up your work area so tools and parts are within easy reach.
Adjust the height of tables, chairs, or platforms when you can, so you work at about elbow level.
Keep heavy items between waist and shoulder height.
Use mats, anti-fatigue flooring, or footrests if your site has them.
Report work setups that cause pain so they can be fixed.
must_say: Set up your work area before you start, so you are not reaching, bending, or twisting all shift.
never_say: Your body will adjust to any work setup.
There is nothing you can change about your work area.
Back pain is just part of the job.
story_seed: A worker on a new line kept reaching over a bin to grab parts and started having shoulder pain. Moving the bin closer fixed the reach in a few minutes.
crew_questions: What part of your work area makes you reach, bend, or twist the most?
Who do you tell here when a workstation needs to be adjusted?

title: Workplace violence warning signs
hazard: Threats, fights, and attacks at work can cause serious injury or death, and they often follow warning signs.
key_points: Get away to a safe place and call 911 if someone has a weapon or is attacking.
Report threats, harassment, or scary behavior to your supervisor or security right away.
Notice warning signs like angry outbursts, threats, or talk of hurting others.
Never try to calm down or confront an armed or violent person yourself.
Know your site's emergency plan, exits, and how to call for help.
must_say: If someone has a weapon or is attacking, get away and call 911.
Report every threat. Never keep a threat to yourself.
never_say: Ignore threats; they are just people blowing off steam.
Step in and wrestle a weapon away from someone.
Only report violence after someone gets hurt.
story_seed: A worker heard a coworker make a threat about a supervisor after a write-up. She reported it to security, who followed the site's plan before anything happened.
crew_questions: Who would you tell here if a coworker made a threat?
Do you know the exits and how to call for help from your work area?

title: Working impaired
hazard: Working under the influence of alcohol, drugs, some medicines, or extreme tiredness slows reactions and judgment, putting you and others at risk.
key_points: Never run machines, drive, or work at heights while impaired.
Tell your supervisor if a medicine makes you sleepy or dizzy, before you start work.
Speak up to a supervisor if a coworker seems impaired and could get hurt.
Follow your site's policy on alcohol, drugs, and medicines.
Use your site's employee help program if you or someone you know needs support.
must_say: Never run equipment or drive while impaired. Tell your supervisor before you start.
never_say: A little alcohol before a shift is fine if you feel okay.
Prescription medicine is always safe to work on.
Covering for an impaired coworker is being a good friend.
story_seed: A worker took a new cold medicine and felt foggy at the start of shift. He told his lead before he got on the forklift.
crew_questions: What would you do if a coworker showed up and did not seem right?
Do you know where to find our site's help program?

title: Permit-required confined spaces
hazard: Confined spaces like tanks, pits, and bins can hold bad air, trap people, or bury them in loose material, and can kill in minutes.
key_points: Never go in after someone who collapses inside a confined space; call trained rescue and 911.
Never enter a permit space unless you are trained, authorized, and the entry permit is complete.
Learn which spaces at your site are permit spaces; if a tank, pit, or bin is not marked, ask before entering.
Follow your site's entry permit and procedure every time.
Make sure an attendant is outside and rescue is set up before anyone goes in.
Get out right away if the attendant tells you to or you notice warning signs.
must_say: Never enter a permit space unless you are trained and the permit is complete.
If someone collapses inside, do not go in. Call trained rescue and 911.
never_say: A quick look inside a tank doesn't need a permit.
If the air smells fine, it is safe to go in.
Anyone can go in to help a coworker who collapses inside.

facts.text: A confined space is big enough to bodily enter, has limited ways in or out, and is not designed for people to be in all the time.
A permit space is a confined space with extra hazards, such as bad air, material that can bury you, a shape that can trap you, or another serious hazard.
Employers must tell workers about permit spaces, for example with a sign reading 'DANGER - PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER.'

story_seed: A worker was about to climb into a hopper to clear a jam. A coworker pointed to the danger sign and stopped him until the entry permit, air test, and attendant were in place.
crew_questions: Which spaces on our site are permit spaces?
What would stop you from going in, even if someone asked you to hurry?

title: The attendant's job
hazard: If the attendant gets distracted or goes inside, entrants in trouble may not get out, and the attendant can become a second victim.
key_points: Call for rescue right away if an entrant may need help getting out; do not go in.
Stay outside the space for the whole entry until another attendant relieves you.
Keep an accurate count of who is inside at all times.
Order everyone out right away if you see a problem inside or outside the space.
Keep unauthorized people away from the space.
Do no other work that pulls your attention from the entrants.
must_say: Attendants stay outside. If entrants need help, call rescue. Never go in.
never_say: The attendant can step away for a minute if things look fine.
If an entrant collapses, the attendant should go in after them.
The attendant can help with other work while watching.

facts.text: The attendant must stay outside the permit space during entry until relieved by another attendant.
The attendant must keep an accurate count of entrants and order them out if a problem is detected inside or outside the space.
The attendant must call rescue and emergency services as soon as entrants may need help to escape.

story_seed: An attendant noticed an entrant's voice sounded slurred over the radio. She ordered everyone out right away and called for the rescue team instead of going in herself.
crew_questions: What do our attendants use to keep track of who is inside?
How would our attendant call rescue from each permit space we have?

title: Testing the air before entry
hazard: The air inside a confined space can lack oxygen or hold flammable or toxic gases you cannot see or smell, and it can kill quickly.
key_points: Never enter until the air has been tested and the permit says it is safe.
Make sure the air is tested in order by a trained tester: oxygen first, then flammable gases, then toxic gases.
Keep testing or monitoring during the job as your permit requires.
Get out right away if the alarm sounds or conditions change.
Ask to watch the air testing; entrants must be given the chance to see it.
Follow your site's procedure for the meter and its checks.
must_say: Never enter a confined space until the air is tested and the permit says it is safe.
never_say: If you can't smell anything, the air is safe.
One test in the morning is good for the whole day no matter what.
Sniff the air at the opening to check it.

facts.text: Before entry, the permit space must be tested to see if conditions are acceptable, and each entrant must be given the chance to watch the testing.
When testing the air, test first for oxygen, then for combustible gases and vapors, then for toxic gases and vapors.
Oxygen below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent is a hazardous atmosphere.

story_seed: A crew was ready to enter a tank that had been cleaned the day before. The air meter showed low oxygen, and the entry was stopped until the space was ventilated and retested.
crew_questions: Who tests the air on our permit spaces, and how is the meter checked?
What would you do if the alarm went off while you were inside?

title: Don't become the second victim
hazard: People who rush into a confined space to save a coworker are often overcome by the same hazard and die too.
key_points: Never go into a confined space to rescue someone; call for trained rescue and 911.
Use the retrieval line from outside if your site's rescue plan allows it.
Keep others from going in.
Know how to call rescue from each permit space before entry starts.
Follow your site's rescue plan.
must_say: Never go in after a downed coworker. Call trained rescue and 911.
Do not become the second victim.
never_say: Hold your breath and go in to pull them out.
Anyone nearby should jump in to help.
A dust mask is enough to go in for a quick rescue.

facts.text: Retrieval systems must be used when an entrant goes into a permit space, unless they would increase the overall risk or would not help a rescue.
A mechanical device must be available to pull people out of vertical permit spaces more than 5 feet deep.
Rescue team members must practice permit space rescues at least once every 12 months.

story_seed: A worker saw a coworker slump at the bottom of a pit. He started down the ladder, but the attendant stopped him, called rescue, and began cranking the retrieval line.
crew_questions: Who is our rescue team for permit spaces, and how do we call them?
What would make it hard not to rush in, and how can we stop each other?

title: Hand tools
hazard: Broken or misused hand tools can slip, break, or send pieces flying, causing cuts, eye injuries, and bruises.
key_points: Inspect hand tools before use and tag out ones with cracked handles, mushroomed heads, or worn jaws.
Use the right tool for the job; never use a screwdriver as a pry bar or chisel.
Wear safety glasses when striking, cutting, or chipping.
Carry and store sharp tools so edges are covered or pointed down.
Never use compressed air to clean off your clothes or skin.
must_say: Inspect every tool before you use it. If it is damaged, tag it out.
never_say: A taped-up handle is as good as new.
Any tool works if you push hard enough.
Your own tools from home are not the company's concern.

facts.text: The employer is responsible for the safe condition of tools used at work, including tools that workers bring from home.
Compressed air may only be used for cleaning when reduced to less than 30 psi, and only with chip guarding and protective gear (PPE).

story_seed: A worker grabbed a hammer with a cracked handle to free a stuck part. A coworker noticed the crack, swapped in a good hammer, and tagged the broken one out.
crew_questions: Where do we send damaged hand tools here?
Which jobs tempt people to use the wrong tool?

title: Portable power tools
hazard: Power tools can cut, crush, shock, or throw debris, and a missing guard or bad cord can cause serious injury.
key_points: Inspect the tool, cord, and guard before each use; remove damaged tools from service.
Never remove, pin back, or tie back a guard.
Unplug or disconnect the tool before changing blades, bits, or wheels.
Keep both hands and body out of the line of the blade or bit.
Wear eye protection and other protective gear (PPE) your site requires.
Follow your site's procedure for cords and ground fault protection.
must_say: Never remove or tie back a guard on a power tool.
never_say: It's fine to pin the lower guard on a circular saw so it cuts faster.
Tape on a damaged cord makes it safe.
You can change a blade while the tool is plugged in if the switch is off.

facts.text: Hand-held circular saws with blades over 2 inches must have guards above and below the base plate, and the lower guard must return to cover the blade automatically.
All cracked saws must be removed from service.
The on/off control on hand-held power tools must be placed to reduce the chance of turning it on by accident.

story_seed: A worker found a circular saw with its lower guard wedged open. He took it out of service and reported it before anyone used it.
crew_questions: Which power tools here get the most wear and need the closest checks?
How do we tag and remove a damaged tool on our site?

title: Knives and box cutters
hazard: Knives and box cutters can slip and cause deep cuts to hands, legs, and arms.
key_points: Cut away from your body and keep your free hand out of the cutting path.
Use a sharp blade; dull blades take more force and slip more.
Use self-retracting or safety cutters if your site provides them.
Retract or cover the blade every time you set it down.
Wear the cut-resistant gloves your site requires for cutting tasks.
Throw out used blades in the container your site provides.
must_say: Always cut away from your body, and keep your other hand out of the path.
never_say: A dull blade is safer than a sharp one.
Pull the blade toward you for better control.
Leave the blade out so it's ready to use.
story_seed: A worker cutting shrink wrap pulled the knife toward his leg and the blade skipped. It caught his pants, not his leg, and he started cutting away from his body after that.
crew_questions: Which cutting jobs here are the most awkward?
Do we have the right cutters and gloves for the jobs we do?

title: Cut-off saws and abrasive wheels
hazard: Abrasive wheels spin very fast and can shatter, throwing pieces that cause serious injuries to the face, eyes, and body.
key_points: Inspect every wheel and do a ring test before mounting it.
Check that the tool's speed does not exceed the speed marked on the wheel.
Keep the guard in place and adjusted between you and the wheel.
Stand out of the path of the wheel when starting the tool.
Wear eye and face protection your site requires.
Use only the wheel type made for your tool and task.
must_say: Never use a grinder or cut-off saw without its guard in place.
never_say: You can take the guard off to reach a tight spot.
Any wheel that fits the spindle is okay to use.
A cracked wheel is fine if the crack is small.

facts.text: Right before mounting, every wheel must be closely inspected and sounded by the user (a ring test) to check for damage.
The spindle speed of the machine must be checked so it does not exceed the maximum speed marked on the wheel.
Guards on right angle (vertical) portable grinders must be placed between the operator and the wheel during use.

story_seed: A worker grabbed a cut-off wheel from a drawer and almost mounted it on a faster grinder. A coworker checked the speed marking, and the wheel was swapped for the right one.
crew_questions: How do we store wheels here so they don't get damaged?
Who checks that wheels and tools are matched for speed?

title: Stop work authority
hazard: When people keep working through an unsafe condition because they feel they can't stop, someone can get hurt.
key_points: Stop the job right away if you see a hazard that could hurt someone.
Tell the people involved and your supervisor why you stopped.
Make the area safe or keep people away until the hazard is fixed.
Restart only after the hazard is fixed and the crew agrees it is safe.
Follow your site's stop work procedure, and ask your supervisor who can stop a job at your site.
Thank people who stop work, even when it turns out to be okay.
must_say: If something looks unsafe, stop first, then talk.
never_say: You'll get in trouble for stopping work if it turns out fine.
Finish the job first, then report the hazard.
Keep working and hope it is fine.
story_seed: A new worker saw a load swinging close to people and called out to stop. The crane operator paused, the area was cleared, and the lift was replanned.
crew_questions: What would make it hard to stop work here?
When was the last time someone stopped a job here, and what happened?

title: Speaking up about a hazard
hazard: Hazards that people see but don't mention stay in place until they hurt someone.
key_points: Shout 'Stop!' first if someone is about to get hurt; skip the polite words and explain after.
Tell the person directly and kindly what you see.
Report hazards to your supervisor and follow your site's reporting process.
Listen and say thanks when someone points out a hazard to you.
Follow up if a hazard you reported is not fixed.
must_say: If you see something unsafe, say something. Speak up now, not later.
never_say: It's not your place to say anything.
If no one else is worried, it must be fine.
Speaking up is snitching.
story_seed: A worker saw a coworker about to climb a damaged ladder. She spoke up, offered a good ladder, and they tagged the broken one out together.
crew_questions: What makes it hard to speak up here?
How do you want people to tell you when they see you doing something unsafe?

title: Line of fire
hazard: Workers get struck, crushed, or caught when they are in the path of moving equipment, falling objects, or released energy.
key_points: Stay out of the path of moving vehicles, loads, and machine parts.
Never stand under a suspended load.
Keep out of the path of anything under tension or pressure, like straps, springs, and hoses.
Never put your hands or body between moving and fixed objects.
Stop and move out of the path if equipment or loads start to move.
must_say: Stay out of the path. Things that move, fall, or snap do not go where you expect.
never_say: Just know where it will go and you'll be fine.
Quick reflexes will keep you safe.
Standing under a load is okay if it's only for a second.
story_seed: A worker stood right behind a strap being tightened on a load. The strap snapped, but he had just stepped aside after a coworker told him to move out of the path.
crew_questions: Where on our site are people most often in the line of fire?
What equipment here stores energy that could suddenly release?

title: Plan the job before you start
hazard: Jumping into a job without planning means hazards get missed until someone gets hurt.
key_points: Walk the work area and look for hazards before you start.
Talk through the steps, the hazards, and the controls with your crew.
Check that you have the right tools, protective gear (PPE), and permits.
Stop and re-plan if the job or conditions change.
Follow your site's pre-task planning form or process.
must_say: Plan the job before you start, and stop to re-plan if anything changes.
never_say: Planning is a waste of time on simple jobs.
Experienced workers don't need to plan.
Once the plan is written, never change it.
story_seed: Before moving a heavy part, a crew talked through the job and spotted that the path was blocked. They cleared it first instead of finding out halfway through.
crew_questions: Which jobs here change the most once we get started?
What's one hazard we have missed in past plans?

title: Shift handoff
hazard: When important safety information is not passed between shifts, the next crew can walk into hazards they don't know about.
key_points: Tell the next shift about any open hazards, locked-out equipment, or unfinished work.
Use your site's handoff log or checklist.
Ask questions if something in the handoff is not clear.
Walk the area together for jobs that are risky or not finished.
Never assume equipment is safe because it was safe last shift.
Follow your site's lockout procedure at shift change; never remove another person's lock.
must_say: Tell the next shift about every open hazard and unfinished job.
never_say: The next shift will figure it out.
If it's not written down, it doesn't matter.
Equipment that was safe last shift is safe now.

facts.text: Lockout programs must use specific procedures at shift or personnel changes so lockout protection continues, including an orderly transfer of locks or tags between off-going and oncoming workers.

story_seed: A night crew left a machine with its guard off while waiting for a repair part. The day crew lead asked about it during the handoff and made sure the machine stayed locked out until the guard was back on.
crew_questions: What information most often gets lost between our shifts?
How could we make our handoff easier and clearer?

title: Looking out for new workers
hazard: New workers don't yet know the hazards, shortcuts, and warning signs of a site, so they are more likely to get hurt.
key_points: Show new workers the hazards, exits, and emergency steps in your area.
Watch new workers do a task before leaving them alone.
Tell new workers it is okay to ask questions and stop work.
Speak up kindly when you see a new worker doing something unsafe.
Follow your site's training and mentoring process.
must_say: Look out for new workers. Show them the hazards and tell them they can always ask.
never_say: New workers should figure it out on their own.
Show them the shortcuts so they can keep up.
Asking questions means they can't do the job.
story_seed: A new hire was about to reach into a conveyor to clear a jam. A veteran worker stopped him and showed him how to lock it out the way the site's procedure says before clearing it.
crew_questions: What do you wish someone had told you on your first week here?
How do we pair new workers with experienced ones?

title: Safety signs and tags
hazard: Ignoring or removing safety signs and tags can expose people to hazards they don't know are there.
key_points: Read and follow every danger and caution sign and tag.
Never remove a tag unless you are the person allowed to by your site's procedure.
Report missing, damaged, or hard-to-read signs and tags.
Ask your supervisor if you don't understand a sign or tag.
must_say: Never ignore or remove a danger tag. Follow it every time.
never_say: Tags are just suggestions.
If you know the hazard, you can ignore the sign.
Anyone can take off a tag once the work looks done.

facts.text: Danger signs mean immediate danger and that special precautions are needed; caution signs mean a possible hazard.
Tags must have a signal word, like Danger or Caution, and a message about the hazard or the instruction.
Tags must be used until the hazard is gone or the hazardous job is done.

story_seed: A worker saw a 'Do Not Use' tag on a hand truck and almost used it anyway to save time. A coworker reminded him, and they found a cracked axle when they looked closer.
crew_questions: Which signs or tags here get ignored most?
Who do we tell when a sign is missing or damaged?

title: Contractors on your site
hazard: Contractors may not know your site's hazards, and your crew may not know theirs, which can lead to someone starting equipment someone else is working on.
key_points: Never remove, move, or work around a contractor's lock or tag.
Tell contractors about hazards in your area before they start.
Ask contractors what they are working on and what is locked out.
Follow your site's procedure for working with contractors.
Report contractors working unsafely to your supervisor.
must_say: Never remove or work around anyone's lock or tag, including a contractor's.
never_say: Contractors are on their own; their safety isn't our problem.
It's okay to start equipment if the contractor seems done.
Contractor locks don't count on our machines.

facts.text: When outside contractors do work covered by the lockout rule, the site and the contractor must tell each other their lockout or tagout procedures.
The site must make sure its own workers understand and follow the contractor's lockout rules.

story_seed: A worker was about to restart a conveyor when he saw a lock he didn't recognize. He checked and found a contractor still working inside the guard.
crew_questions: How do we let our crew know when contractors are working in our area?
What do we do if we find a contractor's lock and can't find the contractor?
